t: An angel promises John the Baptist's birth
s: The priest Zechariah is serving in the temple when Gabriel tells him that his aged wife Elizabeth will bear the forerunner of the Lord.

t: The angel Gabriel appears to Mary
s: Mary, engaged to Joseph, is told she will conceive and bear the Son of the Most High, and she answers, “Let it be to me according to your word.”

t: Mary visits Elizabeth
p: Ein Karem, hill country of Judea
s: Mary travels south to Elizabeth, whose baby leaps at her greeting, and Mary answers with the song traditionally called the Magnificat.
n: The hill-country town is not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.

t: John the Baptist is born
s: Elizabeth's son is born and named John, and Zechariah, able to speak again, prophesies about his son and the coming salvation.
n: Town not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.

t: Jesus is born in Bethlehem
s: Because of a Roman census Joseph and Mary go to David's town, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.

t: Shepherds and the angels
s: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields that a Savior has been born, and the shepherds go and find the baby.
n: Traditional site near Beit Sahour; the fields are not named.

t: The Magi visit Jesus
s: Eastern wise men follow a star, ask Herod in Jerusalem where the king of the Jews is to be born, and worship the child with gifts.

t: Jesus presented in the Temple
s: Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple, where Simeon and Anna recognize him as the promised salvation.

t: The flight to Egypt
s: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
n: Exact place in Egypt is not given; this pin marks the country generally.

t: Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
s: Herod, tricked by the Magi, orders the boys of Bethlehem killed, which Matthew links to Jeremiah's mourning at Ramah.

t: The family settles in Nazareth
s: After Herod's death the family returns from Egypt and makes its home in Galilee, in Nazareth.

t: The boy Jesus in the Temple
s: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents find him listening to the teachers and asking questions.

t: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness
s: John calls Israel to repent and be baptized, and says that someone far greater is coming after him.
n: Traditionally Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas); the exact spot is debated.

t: Jesus is baptized
s: Jesus is baptized by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice calls him his beloved Son.
n: Traditional site; the exact location is debated.

t: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
s: After forty days of fasting, Jesus resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Scripture.
n: Traditional Mount of Temptation near Jericho; the wilderness spot is not named.

t: The first disciples follow Jesus
s: Andrew, another disciple, Peter, Philip and Nathanael begin following Jesus after John points him out as the Lamb of God.
n: Site debated.

t: The wedding at Cana
s: At a village wedding Jesus turns water into wine, the first of the signs John records.
n: Kafr Kanna is the traditional site; Khirbet Qana is another candidate.

t: Jesus clears the Temple (first Passover)
s: Jesus drives out the money changers and sellers and speaks of raising up the temple of his body in three days.

t: Nicodemus visits Jesus at night
s: A Pharisee and member of the council comes by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God so loved the world.
n: Exact house not named.

t: Jesus and John both baptize
s: Jesus' disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes at Aenon, and John says of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
n: Site debated.

t: The woman at the well
s: Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for water and offers her living water, and many in the town come to believe.

t: Jesus heals an official's son
s: A royal official begs Jesus to heal his dying son at Capernaum, and Jesus says, “Go; your son will live,” from Cana.

t: Jesus moves to Capernaum
s: Hearing that John has been arrested, Jesus goes to Galilee and makes Capernaum his base, preaching that the kingdom is near.

t: Jesus is rejected at Nazareth
s: In his hometown synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah and says it is fulfilled today, but the people turn against him.

t: Jesus calls the first fishermen
s: Jesus calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to leave their nets and follow him, and Luke places this after a huge catch of fish.
n: Luke names the lake of Gennesaret; the exact shore is not named.

t: Authority in the Capernaum synagogue
s: Jesus teaches with authority and drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the synagogue.

t: Peter's mother-in-law and the evening healings
s: Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law, and that evening the whole town gathers at the door for healing.

t: A preaching tour of Galilee
s: Jesus travels through the towns of Galilee teaching, preaching and healing, and large crowds follow him.
n: Region marker; no single town.

t: Jesus cleanses a leper
s: A man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Jesus touches him and heals him.
n: Town not named.

t: The paralytic lowered through the roof
s: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof, and Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.

t: Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners
s: Jesus calls the tax collector Levi (Matthew) and dines with tax collectors and sinners, saying he came for the sick.

t: Healing at the pool of Bethesda
s: On a Sabbath Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, then explains his relationship to the Father.

t: Lord of the Sabbath in the grainfields
s: When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath.
n: Field not named.

t: The man with the withered hand
s: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath in a synagogue, and his opponents begin to plot against him.
n: Town not named.

t: Jesus chooses the Twelve
s: After a night in prayer, Jesus names twelve disciples as apostles.
n: The mountain is not named.

t: The Sermon on the Mount
s: Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer and much more; Luke's parallel is set on a level place.
n: Traditional site.

t: The centurion's servant
s: A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant without coming to his house, and Jesus marvels at his faith.

t: Jesus raises a widow's son
s: At the gate of Nain Jesus stops a funeral and tells a widow's dead son to rise.

t: Accused of working by Beelzebul
s: After a healing, Jesus' critics say he casts out demons by the prince of demons, and he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand.
n: Setting is “the house” in Mark.

t: Jesus' true family
s: When his mother and brothers come for him, Jesus says that those who do God's will are his family.

t: Parables by the sea
p: Shore of the Sea of Galilee
s: From a boat Jesus teaches the crowds in parables, including the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed and the yeast.
n: Traditional spot at Tabgha.

t: Jesus calms the storm
s: A violent squall hits the boat, and Jesus calms the wind and waves with a word.

t: The Gerasene demoniac
p: Kursi, east shore of the lake
s: Jesus frees a man from a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the lake.
n: Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes appear in the manuscripts; Kursi is the usual site.

t: Jairus' daughter and the woman with bleeding
s: On the way to Jairus' house a woman is healed by touching Jesus' cloak, and Jesus then raises Jairus' daughter.
n: Town implied by the context.

t: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum
s: Jesus warns the towns where most of his miracles were done that they will face judgment if they do not repent.

t: The Twelve are sent out
s: Jesus sends the Twelve in pairs to preach and heal, with instructions about what to carry and how to respond to rejection.
n: Region marker.

t: John the Baptist is imprisoned and killed
s: Herod Antipas imprisons John for rebuking his marriage, and John is beheaded at Herodias' request.
n: Josephus names Machaerus as the prison; the Gospels do not.

t: Jesus feeds the five thousand
s: With five loaves and two fish Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men, the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.
n: Luke names Bethsaida; the exact site is debated.

t: Jesus walks on the water
s: Jesus comes to the disciples across the stormy lake, and Peter briefly walks toward him.

t: Healing at Gennesaret
s: People bring the sick to touch the edge of Jesus' cloak, and all who touch him are healed.

t: The Bread of Life
s: The crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum, and he says he is the bread of life; many disciples turn back at this teaching.

t: What defiles a person
s: Pharisees ask why the disciples ignore tradition, and Jesus says what defiles a person comes from the heart.
n: Place not named.

t: The Syrophoenician woman's faith
s: Jesus enters Gentile territory, and a woman's persistent faith leads him to heal her daughter.

t: Healing the deaf man in the Decapolis
s: Jesus heals a deaf man who could hardly speak, and many other sick people, in Gentile country.
n: Region marker.

t: Jesus feeds the four thousand
s: A second large crowd is fed with seven loaves and a few fish.
n: Exact site not named.

t: Pharisees demand a sign
s: Jesus lands at Magadan (Magdala or Dalmanutha) and refuses the Pharisees' request for a sign.
n: Mark's Dalmanutha is uncertain.

t: A blind man healed at Bethsaida
s: Jesus heals a blind man in two stages, in a story only Mark records.

t: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi
s: Peter says Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to speak of his coming suffering.

t: The Transfiguration
s: On a high mountain Jesus shines with glory and speaks with Moses and Elijah, and the Father calls him his Son.
n: Tradition favors Tabor; some scholars prefer Mount Hermon.

t: Jesus heals a boy with a spirit
s: Jesus casts out a spirit that the disciples could not, saying some kinds need prayer.
n: Place not named.

t: The temple tax and the coin in the fish
s: Asked about the temple tax, Jesus sends Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth.

t: Teaching on greatness and forgiveness
s: The disciples argue about who is greatest, and Jesus teaches humility, care for little ones and forgiveness.

t: Jesus teaches at the Feast of Tabernacles
s: At the autumn feast Jesus teaches in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to him, and sends away the accusers of a woman caught in adultery.

t: “I am the light of the world”
s: Jesus says he is the light of the world and that before Abraham was, he is.

t: The man born blind
s: Jesus sends a blind man to wash at Siloam and he sees, which leads to a sharp dispute with the Pharisees.

t: The Good Shepherd
s: Jesus says he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
n: Setting continues from the Jerusalem feast.

t: Samaritan village refuses Jesus
s: Setting his face toward Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village, and he rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire.
n: Village not named.

t: The seventy-two are sent out
s: Jesus sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs, and they return with joy.
n: Region marker.

t: The Good Samaritan
s: Asked who his neighbor is, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who helps a man beaten on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.
n: Told as a parable on the road down to Jericho.

t: Martha and Mary
s: Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.
n: Luke says only “a village”; Bethany is the traditional identification.

t: Feast of Dedication
s: At the winter feast Jesus says he and the Father are one, and the crowd tries to stone him.

t: Raising of Lazarus
s: Jesus weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb after four days.

t: The plot to kill Jesus
s: After Lazarus is raised, the chief priests and Caiaphas decide Jesus must die.

t: Jesus withdraws to Ephraim
s: Because of the plot, Jesus leaves public view and stays with his disciples in a town called Ephraim.
n: Site identified with et-Taybeh.

t: Ten lepers cleansed
s: Ten men with leprosy are healed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.

t: Teaching about divorce
s: Pharisees test Jesus about divorce, and he points back to God's design in creation.
n: Region marker.

t: Jesus blesses the children
s: Jesus welcomes children and says the kingdom belongs to such as these.
n: Region marker.

t: The rich young ruler
s: A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and goes away sad when Jesus tells him to sell all.
n: Region marker.

t: Third prediction of the Passion
s: Jesus tells the Twelve for the third time that he will be killed and rise, and he teaches that greatness is serving.
n: Region marker.

t: Blind Bartimaeus
s: As Jesus leaves Jericho a blind beggar cries out to him and receives his sight.
n: Matthew mentions two men.

t: Zacchaeus
s: Jesus invites himself to the house of the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, who gives half his goods to the poor.

t: Mary anoints Jesus at Bethany
s: A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus shortly before his death, and he says she has prepared him for burial.
n: Matthew and Mark place it in the house of Simon the leper.

t: The Triumphal Entry
p: Bethphage and the Mount of Olives
s: Riding a donkey, Jesus enters Jerusalem to cries of “Hosanna” from the crowds.

t: The fig tree cursed
s: Jesus curses a fruitless fig tree, and the next day it has withered; he uses this to teach about faith.

t: Jesus clears the Temple (last week)
s: Jesus overturns the money changers' tables, saying the temple should be a house of prayer.

t: Questions and teaching in the Temple
s: Leaders challenge Jesus' authority, and he answers about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment.

t: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus
s: Greeks come to Philip wanting to see Jesus, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die and of being lifted up.

t: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees
s: Jesus sharply warns against the religious leaders' hypocrisy and laments over Jerusalem.

t: The widow's offering
s: Jesus watches the crowd give and says a poor widow gave more than all the rest.

t: The Olivet Discourse
s: On the Mount of Olives Jesus speaks of the temple's fall, coming trials and his return, and tells parables about being ready.

t: Judas agrees to betray Jesus
s: Judas goes to the chief priests and agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.

t: The Last Supper
s: At the Passover meal Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives them the bread and cup, and says one of them will betray him.
n: Traditional site of the Upper Room.

t: The farewell discourse
s: Jesus comforts his disciples, promises the Spirit and says he is the vine and they are the branches.
n: Traditional site; the last parts are spoken on the way.

t: Jesus' prayer for his followers
s: Jesus prays for himself, his disciples and all who will believe through them.
n: Exact place not named; spoken before crossing the Kidron.

t: Gethsemane
s: Jesus prays in agony in the garden, asking that the cup pass but submitting to the Father's will.

t: Jesus is arrested
s: Judas leads a crowd with swords and clubs to arrest Jesus, and the disciples flee.

t: Jesus before the high priest; Peter denies him
s: Jesus is questioned by Annas and Caiaphas while Peter denies knowing him three times.
n: Traditional location.

t: The death of Judas
s: Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the silver and takes his own life, and the priests buy a field with the money.
n: Traditional site of Akeldama.

t: Jesus before Pilate
s: Pilate questions Jesus, finds no guilt, and finally gives him up to be crucified.
n: The location of the praetorium is debated.

t: Jesus before Herod Antipas
s: Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, who mocks him and sends him back.
n: Place of Herod's stay is not named.

t: The road to Golgotha
s: Soldiers mock Jesus, and Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross.

t: The Crucifixion
s: Jesus is crucified between two criminals, forgives those who killed him, and dies.
n: Traditional site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

t: The burial of Jesus
s: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay Jesus in a new tomb, and a guard is set.

t: The empty tomb
s: Women find the tomb empty, and Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus.

t: The road to Emmaus
s: The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and is recognized when he breaks bread.
n: Site debated; Emmaus-Qubeibeh is one candidate.

t: Jesus appears in the upper room
s: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and side, and opens the Scriptures to them.
n: Setting is a locked room; the traditional site is the Upper Room.

t: Thomas sees the risen Jesus
s: A week later Jesus appears to Thomas, who says, “My Lord and my God!”

t: Breakfast by the lake
s: The risen Jesus cooks breakfast for seven disciples on the shore and restores Peter.
n: Traditional spot at Tabgha.

t: The Great Commission
s: Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain and sends them to make disciples of all nations.
n: Mountain not named.

t: The Ascension
s: Jesus blesses the disciples and is taken up into heaven.
n: Luke says near Bethany; Acts 1 names the Mount of Olives.

t: Jesus’ last words and the promise of the Spirit
s: For forty days the risen Jesus teaches the apostles about the kingdom, tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into a cloud. Two angels say he will return the same way.
n: Luke's Gospel ends with the Ascension near Bethany; Acts names the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day's walk from the city.

t: The believers pray and choose Matthias
s: About 120 believers wait and pray together. Peter reads Judas's fall in the Psalms, and the lot falls to Matthias to join the Eleven.
n: The upper room is not located exactly. Tradition points to the Cenacle on Mount Zion.

t: Pentecost: the Spirit comes
s: Wind, fire and many languages. The disciples are filled with the Spirit and Jewish pilgrims from across the world hear God's mighty deeds in their own tongues.
n: Luke does not say where in Jerusalem. A house or the temple courts are both possible.

t: Peter preaches and three thousand are baptized
s: Peter says the crucified Jesus is both Lord and Messiah, quotes Joel and David, and calls the crowd to repent. About three thousand are baptized that day.
n: The southern steps and the many ritual baths found beside them make this a likely setting, but Luke does not name the spot.

t: The first church shares life together
s: The new believers learn from the apostles, break bread in homes, pray, and share their goods with anyone in need.

t: A lame man healed at the Beautiful Gate
s: Peter and John, going up to the three o'clock prayer, tell a man lame from birth to walk in the name of Jesus. He enters the temple leaping and praising God.
n: The Beautiful Gate is not certainly identified. It was on the east side of the temple complex.

t: Peter preaches in Solomon's Portico
s: A crowd gathers. Peter says God has glorified the Servant they handed over, and calls them to repent so that times of refreshing may come.
n: Solomon's Portico was the covered colonnade on the east side of the temple platform.

t: Peter and John before the council
s: Arrested by the temple guard, the two are questioned by Annas, Caiaphas and the council. Peter answers that there is salvation in no one else. They are warned and released.
n: Exact meeting place not given. The council often met in the temple precincts or at the high priest's house.

t: The church prays and shares
s: The believers pray for boldness, the place shakes, and they are filled again. Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.

t: Ananias and Sapphira
s: A couple sell property and keep back part of the price while claiming to give all of it. Peter exposes the lie, and both die. Great fear falls on the church.

t: The apostles arrested and freed by an angel
s: Many are healed in the shadow of Peter. The high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors at night and sends them back to teach in the temple.

t: Gamaliel's advice to the council
s: The apostles say they must obey God rather than men. The Pharisee Gamaliel urges caution: if this is of God, no one can stop it. They are flogged and released, rejoicing.

t: Seven men chosen to serve
s: Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily food. The apostles ask the church to choose seven, including Stephen and Philip, and the word of God spreads.

t: Stephen before the council
s: Stephen is accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He retells Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon and says the Righteous One has now been betrayed and murdered.

t: Saul's background: born in Tarsus
s: Paul calls himself a Jew born in Tarsus, 'no obscure city.' Tarsus was a major trading and university city in southeastern Asia Minor. He was also a Roman citizen.
n: Acts tells this later, in Paul's own defenses. We place it here as the start of his story.

t: Saul trained under Gamaliel
s: Paul says he grew up in Jerusalem and was trained 'at the feet of Gamaliel,' the same teacher who urged caution in chapter 5. He lived as a strict Pharisee.
n: This is told later in Paul's defenses and placed here to show where he came from.

t: Stephen stoned; Saul watches
p: North of the city wall, Jerusalem
s: Stephen sees the heavens opened and Jesus standing at God's right hand. He is dragged out and stoned, praying for his killers. The witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approves.
n: The place is not named. Tradition has located it at different spots outside the walls.

t: Philip in Samaria
s: Scattered by persecution, Philip preaches in a Samaritan city. Many believe and are baptized. Peter and John come down, and the Spirit is given. Simon the sorcerer offers money for the power and is rebuked.
n: Luke says 'a city of Samaria.' Sebaste, the former capital, is one candidate; the city is not named.

t: Philip and the Ethiopian official
s: An angel sends Philip to a desert road. He meets the treasurer of the Candace of Ethiopia reading Isaiah 53, explains it from the passage, and baptizes him. Philip is then found at Azotus.
n: The spot is unknown. The road from Jerusalem to Gaza is described as 'desert.'

t: Saul sets out to arrest believers
s: Saul drags believers from their homes to prison and asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that he can bring any followers of 'the Way' back in chains.

t: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the Damascus road
s: A light from heaven flashes around Saul and he falls to the ground. A voice says, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' Blinded, he is led by hand into Damascus and fasts three days.
n: Tradition places the meeting near Kawkab, southwest of Damascus. Luke gives no precise spot.

t: Ananias restores Saul's sight
s: The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to Saul, who is praying at Judas's house on Straight Street. Ananias lays hands on him; scales fall from his eyes, and he is baptized.
n: A Roman street (Via Recta) still runs through the old city of Damascus.

t: Saul preaches and escapes in a basket
s: Saul proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. When a plot forms to kill him, friends lower him in a basket through an opening in the wall at night.
n: Paul recalls the same escape in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33.

t: Saul in Jerusalem with Barnabas
s: The disciples fear Saul until Barnabas brings him to the apostles and tells how he met the Lord. Saul speaks boldly, then is sent home to Tarsus when Greek-speaking Jews seek to kill him.
n: Galatians 1:18-24 gives Paul's own account of this visit.

t: Saul at home in Tarsus
s: The quiet years. Saul goes to Tarsus and Syria and Cilicia. Barnabas later comes looking for him.
n: Luke tells almost nothing about these years. Paul mentions them in Galatians 1:21.

t: Peter heals Aeneas at Lydda
s: Peter finds a man named Aeneas who had been bedridden eight years. 'Jesus Christ heals you,' he says, and Aeneas gets up. Many in Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord.

t: Peter raises Tabitha at Joppa
s: A disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas), known for her kindness, dies. Peter kneels, prays, and says 'Tabitha, arise.' She opens her eyes, and Peter stays in Joppa with Simon the tanner.

t: Cornelius's vision at Caesarea
s: A Roman centurion who fears God and prays and gives alms sees an angel in a vision. He is told to send for Simon Peter at Joppa.
n: Caesarea Maritima was the Roman capital of Judea.

t: Peter's rooftop vision
s: On the roof at noon Peter sees a sheet of animals let down from heaven and hears, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.' Three men from Cornelius arrive at the door.
n: Tradition shows a tanner's house near the harbor. Luke gives no street.

t: The Spirit falls on Gentiles at Cornelius's house
s: Peter says he now sees that God shows no partiality. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear, and they are baptized.

t: Peter explains to the church in Jerusalem
s: Believers criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. He tells the whole story, and the church says, 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.'

t: The church in Antioch; 'Christians'
s: Believers scattered after Stephen's death preach to Greeks in Antioch, and many turn to the Lord. Barnabas fetches Saul from Tarsus, and they teach there for a year. Here the disciples are first called Christians.
n: Antioch was the third-largest city in the empire, in what is now southern Turkey.

t: Relief for Judea and Herod's persecution
s: A prophet named Agabus foretells a famine, and Barnabas and Saul carry a gift to Judea. Herod Agrippa I kills James the brother of John and jails Peter, but an angel frees him and he goes to Mark's mother's house.
n: The house of Mary, John Mark's mother, is not located. Tradition points to Mount Zion.

t: Herod Agrippa I dies
s: Herod accepts a crowd's cry that he speaks like a god, and an angel of the Lord strikes him down. The word of God grows and multiplies.
n: Josephus also describes his death at Caesarea in AD 44.

t: Barnabas and Saul sent out
s: While the prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit says, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul.' The church lays hands on them and sends them off. This is the start of the first missionary journey.

t: Cyprus: Salamis
s: From Seleucia the team sails to Cyprus, Barnabas's home island. At Salamis they preach in the synagogues, with John Mark as their helper.

t: Elymas struck blind at Paphos
s: The proconsul Sergius Paulus asks to hear the word of God. A sorcerer named Elymas opposes them and is struck blind. The proconsul believes. From here Luke calls him Paul.
n: A first-century inscription mentions a Sergius Paulus, but the match is debated.

t: Perga: John Mark turns back
s: The team sails to Perga on the south coast of Asia Minor. John Mark leaves them and returns to Jerusalem. Paul later refuses to take him on the second journey.

t: Paul preaches at Pisidian Antioch
s: In the synagogue Paul retells Israel's story to David and declares that through Jesus forgiveness is proclaimed. The next Sabbath the crowds come, many Jews contradict, and Paul turns to the Gentiles. They are driven out.
n: Near modern Yalvaç, Turkey. Not the same as Antioch on the Orontes.

t: Iconium
s: Paul and Barnabas speak so that a great number of Jews and Greeks believe. The city splits, and when a plot to stone them forms, they leave for Lystra and Derbe.
n: Modern Konya.

t: Lystra: the crowd calls them gods
s: Paul heals a man who has never walked. The crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes and tries to offer sacrifices. Paul tells them to turn from these vain things to the living God.
n: The site is a mound near Hatunsaray, south of Konya. An inscription found nearby is dedicated to Zeus and Hermes.

t: Paul stoned at Lystra
s: Jews from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead. The disciples gather around him; he gets up and goes back in.
n: Paul later writes of this beating (2 Corinthians 11:25).

t: Derbe and the return trip
s: The next day Paul and Barnabas go to Derbe, make many disciples, then retrace their steps and appoint elders in every church with prayer and fasting.
n: The site of Derbe is debated. Kerti Hüyük is the leading candidate.

t: Report back at Antioch
s: Paul and Barnabas sail from Attalia, gather the church, and tell how God 'had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.' They stay a long time.

t: The Jerusalem Council
s: Some say Gentile believers must be circumcised. After debate, Peter reminds the council that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles, and James says the prophets agree. They write a letter: no extra burden beyond a few basic requirements.
n: Galatians 2:1-10 may describe the same meeting from Paul's side. Scholars discuss how the two accounts fit.

t: Paul and Barnabas part ways
s: A sharp dispute over taking John Mark ends their partnership. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus; Paul chooses Silas and heads through Syria and Cilicia. This begins the second journey.

t: Timothy joins at Lystra
s: Paul finds a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, well spoken of. Paul has him circumcised and takes him along.

t: The vision of the man of Macedonia
s: Forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia or Bithynia, Paul reaches Troas. In a night vision a man of Macedonia pleads, 'Come over to Macedonia and help us.' The narrative changes to 'we' here.
n: The 'we' passages (16:10-17, 20:5-15, 21:1-18, 27:1-28:16) are usually taken as signs that Luke the writer was present.

t: Lydia at Philippi
s: By the river on the Sabbath, Paul speaks to a group of women. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, opens her heart, and she and her household are baptized.
n: Philippi was a Roman colony. The river is likely the Gangites, west of the city.

t: The Philippian jailer
s: Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit. Her owners drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer asks, 'What must I do to be saved?'
n: Paul claims Roman citizenship the next morning.

t: Riot at Thessalonica
s: For three Sabbaths Paul argues from Scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. A mob accuses the believers of saying there is another king, Jesus.
n: Thessalonica was the capital of the province of Macedonia.

t: The noble-minded Bereans
s: The Bereans receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if these things are so. When agitators come from Thessalonica, Paul is sent to the coast.
n: Modern Veria.

t: Paul at the Areopagus in Athens
s: Distressed by the idols, Paul speaks in the marketplace and then to the Areopagus council. He points to an altar 'to the unknown god,' quotes Greek poets, and says God will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead.
n: The Areopagus is the rocky hill northwest of the Acropolis.

t: Eighteen months in Corinth
s: Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla, tent-makers, and teaches in the synagogue. When opposition rises he moves next door. The Lord says in a night vision, 'I have many in this city who are my people.' Gallio dismisses the charge against him.
n: Gallio's proconsulship, known from an inscription at Delphi, helps date this to about AD 51-52.

t: A vow at Cenchreae; a short stop at Ephesus
s: Paul cuts his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, sails to Ephesus where he reasons in the synagogue, leaves Priscilla and Aquila there, and returns by Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch.
n: The map pin is at Ephesus.

t: Apollos taught in Ephesus
s: Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, preaches fervently but knows only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

t: Paul in Ephesus: the Spirit, Tyrannus, the burning scrolls
s: Paul finds twelve disciples who know only John's baptism and baptizes them in Jesus' name. For two years he teaches in the hall of Tyrannus. Handkerchiefs, exorcists and burned magic scrolls worth fifty thousand silver pieces mark the time.

t: The riot of the silversmiths
s: Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the city. The crowd chants 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours until the town clerk calms them.
n: The great theater still stands and held about 25,000.

t: Eutychus at Troas
s: After travelling through Macedonia and Greece, Paul meets the church at Troas on the first day of the week. A young man named Eutychus falls from a window during his long talk, and Paul raises him.

t: Farewell to the Ephesian elders
s: Paul summons the elders from Ephesus and tells them he is going to Jerusalem bound in the Spirit. 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' They weep, embrace him, and walk him to the ship.

t: Warnings along the way
s: Sailing by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, Paul reaches Tyre. The disciples there warn him through the Spirit not to go on to Jerusalem. The families kneel with him on the beach and pray.

t: Philip's house and Agabus's warning
s: Paul stays with Philip the evangelist and his four prophesying daughters. Agabus binds his own hands with Paul's belt and says the Jews will bind the owner of the belt. Paul says he is ready to die for the Lord.

t: Paul arrested at the temple
s: James and the elders ask Paul to join four men in a vow. Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing Greeks into the sacred area, and drag him out. Roman soldiers rescue him from the mob.
n: A warning stone found in 1871 forbade foreigners from entering the inner court on penalty of death.

t: Paul speaks from the stairs
s: From the barracks steps Paul addresses the crowd in Aramaic and tells his story. At the word 'Gentiles' they erupt. The tribune orders him examined by flogging until Paul says he is a Roman citizen.

t: Before the Sanhedrin
s: Paul splits the council by saying he is on trial for the resurrection of the dead; Pharisees and Sadducees quarrel. That night the Lord says, 'Take courage, for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.'

t: The plot and the night ride
s: Forty men vow not to eat until they kill Paul. His nephew hears and tells the tribune, who sends Paul with 470 soldiers by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea.
n: Antipatris was on the main road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, about halfway.

t: Before Felix
s: The high priest's lawyer Tertullus accuses Paul. Paul replies that he came to worship, not to stir riots, and that the real issue is the resurrection. Felix keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
n: The Roman governor's palace at Caesarea was the former palace of Herod the Great.

t: Before Festus: 'I appeal to Caesar'
s: The new governor Festus asks if Paul will be tried at Jerusalem. Paul, knowing the danger, says 'I appeal to Caesar.' Festus replies, 'To Caesar you shall go.'

t: Before King Agrippa and Bernice
s: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice come to hear him. Paul tells of his Damascus road meeting and his commission, and asks Agrippa, 'Do you believe the prophets?' The king says Paul could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.

t: Setting sail for Rome
s: Paul, other prisoners, Luke and Aristarchus sail under the centurion Julius. At Myra they change to an Alexandrian grain ship and slowly reach Fair Havens on Crete.
n: Fair Havens (Kaloi Limenes) is on the south coast of Crete.

t: The storm and the angel
s: Against Paul's advice the ship leaves for a better harbor. A northeaster seizes it and drives it for fourteen days. An angel tells Paul that all 276 aboard will be saved, and Paul encourages them to eat.
n: The pin marks the small island of Cauda (Gavdos), where the ship was first driven. The route afterwards is a drift.

t: Shipwreck on Malta
s: The ship runs aground on a sandbar and breaks up. All reach shore. A viper bites Paul's hand and he shakes it into the fire; the islanders call him a god. He heals the father of Publius and many others.
n: Malta is the traditional site; some scholars have proposed other islands.

t: Through Puteoli toward Rome
s: After three months they sail in another Alexandrian ship, landing at Puteoli. Believers there host Paul for a week, and brothers from Rome meet him on the Appian Way. Paul thanks God and takes courage.
n: Puteoli (Pozzuoli) was the main port for the Egyptian grain fleet.

t: Paul in Rome
s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders together, explains his appeal, and from morning to evening testifies about the kingdom and Jesus. Then, for two years in his own rented house, he welcomes all who come, 'proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.'
n: Acts ends here with no verdict. Paul's later years come from his letters and from early church tradition.

t: From Jerusalem around to Illyricum
s: Paul says that "from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ." He has aspired to preach "where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else's foundation."
n: Acts never mentions Illyricum (the Roman lands along the Adriatic, later called Dalmatia). It may mark the far edge of his work in Macedonia (Acts 20:1-2). The pin is Salona, the capital of Dalmatia, as a general marker. 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus went to Dalmatia.

t: Macedonia and Achaia give for the poor
s: Paul says Macedonia and Achaia "were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem." He sees it as a debt: if the Gentiles "have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings."
n: 2 Corinthians 8-9 describes the Macedonian gift in more detail, and 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 the plan for Corinth. Acts 20:4 lists the men who went with Paul to carry it. The pin is Thessalonica, a Macedonian capital.

t: Paul writes from Corinth
s: Timothy, Lucius, Jason and Sosipater send greetings. Tertius, "who wrote down this letter," adds his own. "Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church," sends greetings, and so do Erastus, "the city treasurer," and "our brother Quartus."
n: Romans does not name the place where it was written. Corinth fits best: Paul spends three months in Greece in Acts 20:2-3, Phoebe comes from nearby Cenchreae, and a paving stone inscribed "Erastus" lies near the Corinth theater. Most scholars date the letter to the winter of about AD 56-57.

t: Phoebe of Cenchreae
s: Paul commends "our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea" and asks the Romans to "welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints." She "has been a great help to many people, including me."
n: Cenchreae was Corinth's eastern harbor. Phoebe is probably the one who carried the letter to Rome, but Paul does not say so. The Greek word for "servant" is diakonos, which some translations render "deacon."

t: The letter reaches the church in Rome
s: Paul writes "To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints," a church he has not yet visited. In chapter 16 he greets more than twenty people by name, including Prisca and Aquila, "the church that meets at their house," and the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus.
n: Many scholars think the church grew out of Rome's Jewish community and was shaken when Claudius expelled Jews from the city in about AD 49 (Acts 18:2). Jewish believers returned after he died in AD 54, which would explain the strain between Jewish and Gentile believers in chapters 14-15.

t: Be subject to the governing authorities
s: Paul tells the Roman believers to be subject to the governing authorities, to pay taxes, revenue, respect and honor to those who are owed them, and to owe no one anything except love.
n: Nero became emperor in AD 54, and the first years of his reign were stable. Tacitus records that in AD 58 a public outcry over tax collectors led Nero to consider ending indirect taxes. Paul wrote Romans 13 before the persecution of AD 64.

t: The gift goes to Jerusalem
s: Paul says he is "on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there" and asks the Romans to pray "that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there."
n: Acts 24:17 has Paul tell Felix he returned to Jerusalem "to bring alms to my people and to present offerings." Acts does not describe the handing over. His arrest in the temple follows (Acts 21:27-36), so the prayer in Romans 15:31 was answered in a way Paul did not expect.

t: On to Spain by way of Rome
s: Paul says there are "no further opportunities for me in these regions." He hopes "to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey." First he must deliver the gift to Jerusalem.
n: The Bible does not say whether Paul reached Spain. 1 Clement 5 (about AD 95) says he reached "the limit of the west." The pin is Tarraco, the capital of the Roman province, but Romans names no city.

t: Abraham believed God
s: Paul argues that Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God (Genesis 15:6), before he was circumcised and long before the law came. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile.
n: Genesis 15 does not name the place of the vision, but Abraham was then living by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 14:13). The site near Hebron is traditional.

t: Elijah and the seven thousand
s: Paul asks whether God has rejected his people. He recalls Elijah complaining that he alone was left, and God's answer: "I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal." So now too there is a remnant chosen by grace.
n: The story is in 1 Kings 19. Horeb is another name for Sinai, and its exact location is uncertain. Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site.

t: Paul brings the gospel to Corinth
s: Paul reminds the church how he came: "I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling." He "resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified." He laid the foundation, and others are building on it.
n: Acts 18:1-18 tells the same visit. Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, who made tents like him, argued in the synagogue, and stayed a year and a half. A letter of Claudius found at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, which dates the visit to about AD 50-52. Corinth had been rebuilt as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC.

t: Planted by Paul, watered by Apollos
s: Paul writes, "I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow." He treats himself and Apollos as fellow servants, not rivals. At the end of the letter he says he "strongly urged" Apollos to visit Corinth, but Apollos "was not at all inclined to go now."
n: Acts 18:24-19:1 describes Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria who was taught more fully by Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, then crossed to Achaia and helped the believers there. Paul was back in Ephesus by the time Apollos reached Corinth.

t: Paul writes from Ephesus
s: Paul says, "I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me." He sends greetings from "the churches in the province of Asia," and from Aquila and Prisca and "the church that meets at their house."
n: Acts 19 has Paul in Ephesus for about three years (Acts 20:31). Most scholars date 1 Corinthians to about AD 53-55. When Paul asks "If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain?" he may be speaking figuratively. 2 Corinthians 1:8-9 mentions a crisis in Asia that nearly cost him his life.

t: Chloe's household reports quarrels
s: Paul writes, "some from Chloe's household have informed me that there are quarrels among you." Individuals are saying, "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas," or "I follow Christ." He thanks God that he baptized only Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas.
n: Chloe is named nowhere else, and Paul does not say where she lived. Cephas is Peter, though nothing says he visited Corinth. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue in Acts 18:8, and Gaius is probably the host in Romans 16:23.

t: The message of the cross
s: Paul says "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." Christ crucified is "a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles." God chose what is weak, so that no one can boast except in the Lord.
n: Corinth admired polished speakers who traveled from city to city, and Paul answers them directly. Roman writers such as Cicero called crucifixion the cruelest and most shameful form of execution, so a crucified Messiah was a hard message in any city of the empire.

t: A scandal in the church
s: Paul has heard of "sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father's wife." He tells them to expel the man, and says "a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough." He adds, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed."
n: The woman is most likely the man's stepmother (Leviticus 18:8). Paul also mentions an earlier letter (5:9) that has not survived. Some scholars connect this man with the offender in 2 Corinthians 2:5-8, but others disagree.

t: Lawsuits among believers
s: Paul asks, "how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!" He says the saints "will judge the world," and asks, "Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?" He reminds them: "you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified."
n: Cases in a Roman colony were heard by magistrates in the forum, where wealthy patrons tended to have the advantage. The raised platform (bema) in Corinth's forum is where Gallio heard the case against Paul in Acts 18:12-17.

t: Your body is a temple
s: Paul quotes a slogan, "Everything is permissible for me," and answers it. He says "Flee from sexual immorality," and tells them their body "is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you." "You were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body."
n: The hill above Corinth carried a temple of Aphrodite. Strabo says it once had over a thousand temple slaves, but he describes the older Greek city, which Rome destroyed in 146 BC, and how much of that continued in the Roman city is debated. "Bought at a price" is the language of buying a slave.

t: Marriage, singleness and slavery
s: Paul begins, "Now for the matters you wrote about." He gives advice on marriage, divorce and staying single, marking what comes from "the Lord" and what is his own judgment. He tells slaves, "if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity," and says "the time is short."
n: "The present crisis" (7:26) is not explained. Some link it to the famine in Claudius' reign (Acts 11:28), which Tacitus also mentions, but this is a guess. Slavery was common in Corinth, and many believers there would have been slaves or freed slaves.

t: Food sacrificed to idols
s: Paul says "an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one," but warns that "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Believers must not eat in an idol's temple or cause a weaker brother to stumble. In the market, "Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience."
n: Excavations at Corinth uncovered dining rooms with couches in the Asklepieion, a healing sanctuary north of the city, and in the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore on the slope of Acrocorinth. Meat sold in the market often came from temple sacrifices.

t: Run to win
s: Paul says that "in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize." Athletes train "for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable." He says, "I discipline my body and make it my slave."
n: The Isthmian Games were held every two years at the sanctuary of Poseidon, about ten miles east of Corinth. Winners received a wreath of pine or celery. The stadium has been excavated. Paul's time in Corinth may have overlapped with one of the festivals.

t: Warnings from the wilderness
s: Paul recalls that "our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea." He says "that rock was Christ," and warns against idolatry: "The people sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry." He adds that "God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear."
n: The feast and revelry belong to the golden calf at the foot of Sinai (Exodus 32:6). The exact location of Sinai is uncertain. Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site.

t: The Lord's Supper
s: Paul says that when they meet, "it is not the Lord's Supper you eat." Some go ahead without sharing: "While one remains hungry, another gets drunk." He then recalls what he received: the Lord Jesus "on the night He was betrayed, took bread," and "you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes."
n: The church met in homes. A typical Roman dining room held only about nine people reclining, with more in the adjoining courtyard, so wealthier members may have eaten first. This is the oldest written account of the Lord's Supper, earlier than any Gospel.

t: Gifts, one body, and love
s: Paul says "There are different gifts, but the same Spirit," and "Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it." Chapter 13 says "Love is patient, love is kind," and ends: "the greatest of these is love." In chapter 14 he says he would rather "speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue."
n: Mirrors in Paul's day were polished metal, and Corinth was known for its bronze work, so "a dim reflection as in a mirror" (13:12) would have been familiar. Verses 14:34-35 are debated: some manuscripts place them after verse 40, and scholars differ over whether Paul is limiting disorder, quoting a Corinthian slogan, or whether they were added later.

t: What Paul received: Christ died and was raised
s: Paul passes on "as of first importance": that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and "appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve," then to over five hundred, to James, to all the apostles, and "last of all He appeared to me also."
n: Most scholars think the wording of verses 3-5 goes back to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul probably heard it when he spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18). The pin marks where that report began, not where Paul wrote it.

t: If Christ has not been raised
s: Some in Corinth said there is no resurrection. Paul answers: "if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith." Christ is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," and "as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive." At the last trumpet "the dead will be raised imperishable."
n: Greek thought often hoped for the soul to escape the body, and the Athenians mocked Paul's talk of resurrection in Acts 17:32. The practice of being "baptized for the dead" (15:29) is mentioned nowhere else, and scholars offer many explanations. The line "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" echoes Isaiah 22:13.

t: The collection for the saints
s: Paul tells the Corinthians to do as he directed the churches of Galatia: "On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income." He will send their chosen representatives with letters "to carry your gift to Jerusalem."
n: The collection began with the agreement in Galatians 2:10 to "remember the poor." Paul writes more of it in 2 Corinthians 8-9 and Romans 15:25-27, and Acts 20:4 lists the men who traveled with him. The pin is the destination.

t: Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus arrive
s: Paul says "Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia." He is glad that "Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you."
n: These three may have brought the Corinthians' letter (7:1) and carried Paul's reply back. Fortunatus is a Latin name, and Achaicus means "from Achaia." Acts 17:34 names converts in Athens, which was also in Achaia, so "first converts" probably means the first household.

t: Timothy, and the plan to come through Macedonia
s: Paul says "I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord," and asks the church to see that Timothy "has nothing to fear while he is with you." He plans: "After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you."
n: Acts 19:21-22 has Paul send Timothy and Erastus into Macedonia, with plans to go on to Achaia, then Jerusalem, then Rome. Paul later changed his plans, which caused hurt feelings (2 Corinthians 1:15-17). The pin is Philippi, a Macedonian city on his route.

t: Despairing even of life in Asia
s: Paul tells the church, "We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead." He says, "We have this treasure in jars of clay."
n: Paul does not say what happened in the province of Asia. Some link it to the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41), but the letter gives no details, and 1 Corinthians 15:32 and 16:9 show he faced danger and many opponents there. Jars of clay were the everyday containers of his day, cheap and easy to break.

t: A changed plan, and a "Yes" in Christ
s: Paul had planned to visit Corinth twice, "so that you might receive a double blessing," on his way to Macedonia and again on his way back. He did not come, and some said he said "Yes, yes" when he meant "No, no." He answers: "all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ." He says he stayed away "to spare you."
n: In 1 Corinthians 16:5-7 Paul had said he would come through Macedonia. Plans then changed more than once. Silvanus is Silas, who came to Corinth with Timothy (Acts 18:5), and the letter says the three of them preached there.

t: The painful visit
s: Paul writes, "So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you." Later he says, "I already warned you the second time I was with you." The visit that hurt both sides is the second, so the next one will be the third.
n: Acts does not mention this visit. Most scholars place it between 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians, a short trip across the Aegean from Ephesus. The details are not known, but something went badly wrong between Paul and a member or group in the church.

t: The letter written "with many tears"
s: Paul says, "through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you." Later he adds, "Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it."
n: Titus is usually thought to have carried it. This letter has not survived, or it survives in part. Some scholars say it is 1 Corinthians, some say it is lost, and some say it is chapters 10-13 of this letter. The pin at Ephesus is the most likely place it was written, not something the letter says.

t: Forgive the offender
s: Paul writes, "Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you." The majority had punished him enough, so "you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow." He says this is so "that Satan should not outwit us."
n: The offender is not named. Some scholars connect him with the man in 1 Corinthians 5, while others think he insulted Paul during the painful visit. The letter does not decide. Paul asks the church to "reaffirm your love for him."

t: No peace at Troas
s: Paul writes that when he went to Troas "to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord, I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there." He says, "So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia."
n: Troas was the usual port for crossing to Macedonia. Paul wanted news from Corinth so badly that he left an open door. Acts 20:1-2 has him leave Ephesus for Macedonia after the riot, and says nothing of Titus.

t: Titus brings good news in Macedonia
s: Paul says, "when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction—conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus." Titus "told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me."
n: Paul does not name the city where he met Titus. Philippi is a likely guess because Paul had friends there, but Thessalonica and Berea are also possible. Titus is never named in Acts, though he appears often in Paul's letters, and Galatians 2:1-3 shows he was a Gentile.

t: The veil of Moses
s: Paul tells the Corinthians "You yourselves are our letter," written "not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." Moses put a veil over his face, but "whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away."
n: The shining face and veil come from Exodus 34:29-35, when Moses came down from Sinai with the second tablets. The exact location of Sinai is uncertain, and Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site. Paul takes the story as a picture of the old covenant, not as a rebuke of Moses.

t: The judgment seat and the ministry of reconciliation
s: Paul says "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ," and that "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." God "reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation." He adds, "we are ambassadors for Christ."
n: The Greek word for "judgment seat" is bema, the same word Acts 18:12 uses for the platform in Corinth's forum where Gallio sat. Paul's readers walked past a real bema every day. An ambassador, in Roman times, spoke for a ruler who was not present.

t: Open hearts, and a warning about partners
s: Paul says "Our hearts are open wide" and asks the Corinthians to "Open wide your hearts also." He warns, "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers," and asks, "What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God."
n: Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids plowing with an ox and a donkey together, in the picture of a yoke. "Belial" is a Hebrew word for worthlessness that later became a name for the evil one. Some scholars think 6:14-7:1 was inserted from another source, while others say it fits Paul's argument.

t: The Macedonian churches give
s: Paul says that in "the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity." He writes that "they gave according to their ability and even beyond it," and "they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints."
n: The Macedonian churches were at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16-17). The pin is Thessalonica as one of them. Philippians 4:15-16 shows the Philippians had supported Paul before. Romans 15:26 says Macedonia and Achaia both gave.

t: Titus and the brothers are sent ahead
s: Paul writes that he is sending Titus and two other brothers. One "is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel" and was "chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering." Paul says, "We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift."
n: Neither brother is named. Acts 20:4 lists the men who later traveled with Paul to Jerusalem: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus. The pin is Corinth, where the brothers were headed.

t: God loves a cheerful giver
s: Paul says "Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously." He asks each person to "give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver." He ends, "Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!"
n: The gift was for believers in Jerusalem, as in Romans 15:25-27 and 1 Corinthians 16:1-4. Galatians 2:10 says the Jerusalem leaders asked Paul to "remember the poor." Acts 24:17 has Paul say he came to Jerusalem to bring gifts for the poor of his nation. The pin is the destination.

t: Paul answers his critics
s: Paul writes, "I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away." Some said, "His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account." He answers that "the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world."
n: Chapters 10-13 have a sharper tone than chapters 1-9. Some scholars think they come from a different letter, perhaps the "tearful" letter or a later one, while others think Paul changed tone after he heard how part of the church was still resisting. The manuscripts hand them down as one letter.

t: The "super-apostles"
s: Paul fears that "just as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ." Visitors preach "a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed." He calls them "false apostles, deceitful workers," and says "Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light."
n: Who the "super-apostles" were is debated. They were probably Jewish Christian teachers who boasted of their credentials and wanted payment (11:7-12, 20, 22). Paul had preached to Corinth free of charge, and the brothers from Macedonia supplied his needs.

t: Beaten, stoned and shipwrecked
s: Paul answers boasting with a list: "Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea." He adds, "Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches."
n: Acts records only one beating with rods (Philippi, Acts 16:22-23), one stoning (Lystra, Acts 14:19) and the later shipwreck at Malta (Acts 27). The shipwrecks in this list happened before Acts 27, and Acts tells of none. The pin marks the stoning, one of the few items on the list that Acts also describes.

t: Lowered in a basket at Damascus
s: Paul says, "In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp." He tells it at the end of his list of weaknesses.
n: Acts 9:23-25 tells the same escape. Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom from Petra, and some scholars date this escape to about AD 37. Paul tells the story as proof that he boasts in weakness, not as a triumph.

t: Caught up to Paradise, and a thorn in the flesh
s: Paul writes of "a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven." He heard "things that man is not permitted to tell." To keep him humble, "I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away." The answer: "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness."
n: Paul gives no place for the vision. Fourteen years before the letter points to about AD 41-43, when Acts 11:25-26 has him in Tarsus and Antioch. The pin is Corinth, where the letter was read. He never says what the thorn was, and many guesses have been made.

t: The third visit
s: Paul writes, "See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden." He fears "quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder," and asks them, "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith." He ends with the blessing: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you."
n: Acts 20:2-3 says Paul spent three months in Greece, and Romans was written then from Corinth (Romans 16:23). The closing blessing in 13:14 names the Lord Jesus Christ, God and the Holy Spirit. Acts 20:4 lists the men who traveled with him, who may have included the delegates for the collection.

t: Another gospel in Galatia
s: Paul skips his usual thanksgiving: "I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—which is not even a gospel." He says that even "an angel from heaven" who preaches another gospel should be "under a curse."
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. The letter never says where Paul wrote it, and its date is debated. An early date is about AD 48-49, before the Jerusalem Council. A later date is during the third journey.

t: A persecutor called by grace
s: Paul says the gospel was not devised by man: "I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ." He tells how "severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it," and how God "set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by His grace" and was pleased "to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles."
n: Galatians does not name the place or tell the story of the road, which Acts 9 does. The pin is Damascus, the city where Paul says he "later returned" after Arabia (1:17). Paul says he did not rush to consult "flesh and blood."

t: Three years, and Arabia
s: Paul writes that he did not go up to Jerusalem, "but I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus. Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas."
n: Paul says only "Arabia" and gives no town or reason. In his day it meant the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Judea, which Aretas IV ruled (2 Corinthians 11:32). The pin at Petra, its capital, marks the region and is a judgment call. "Three years" may be counted from his call, and ancient counting included part years.

t: Fifteen days with Cephas
s: Paul says he went up "to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother." He adds, "I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie."
n: Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter. Acts 9:26-30 tells of this first visit to Jerusalem from Luke's side, with Barnabas bringing Saul to the apostles. Galatians stresses how short the visit was and how few leaders he met.

t: Syria and Cilicia
s: Paul writes, "Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ." They heard only that "The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy," and "they glorified God because of me."
n: Tarsus, his home city (Acts 21:39), was the main city of Cilicia. Acts 9:30 says the believers sent him to Tarsus, and Acts 11:25-26 has Barnabas fetch him to Antioch. The pin is a judgment call for the two regions.

t: Fourteen years later: the private meeting
s: Paul says, "Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also." He set the gospel he preaches among the Gentiles before the leaders, and "not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek." James, Cephas and John "gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship," and asked only that they "remember the poor."
n: Scholars disagree which visit in Acts this is. Many say the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, and others say the famine visit of Acts 11:30. "Fourteen years" may count from his call or from the first visit, and the answer affects the date of Galatians. The "false brothers" in 2:4 are the same kind of teachers Paul argues against in the rest of the letter.

t: Paul opposes Peter at Antioch
s: Paul says, "When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood to be condemned." Before certain men came from James, Peter "used to eat with the Gentiles," but then "he began to draw back and separate himself." Even Barnabas "was led astray." Paul says, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me."
n: Acts does not tell this episode. Acts 15:35 shows Paul and Barnabas at Antioch after the Council, and Acts 15:36-41 says they parted ways. Paul does not report how Peter answered. "Certain men came from James" does not say James sent them to cause trouble, and Paul does not blame James.

t: "O foolish Galatians"
s: Paul asks, "O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified." He asks one question: "Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?" and "After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?"
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town.

t: Abraham believed God
s: Paul writes, "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." The Scripture "foretold the gospel to Abraham: 'All nations will be blessed through you.'" The promise came first: "The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God."
n: Genesis 15:6 and 12:3 are the verses Paul quotes. Abraham lived near Hebron and Mamre in the Genesis story (Genesis 13:18; 18:1). The 430 years in Galatians 3:17 follows the Greek text of Exodus 12:40, and the Hebrew text counts it differently. The pin is a background pin, not a place Paul mentions.

t: The law as guardian
s: Paul asks, "Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred." He says "we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed," and "the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ."
n: Paul says the law "was administered through angels by a mediator" (3:19), which follows a Jewish tradition that angels were present at Sinai (see also Deuteronomy 33:2, Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2). The exact location of Sinai is uncertain, and Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site. The pin is a background pin. "Guardian" was the household slave who took a child to school.

t: No longer slaves, but sons
s: Paul says "You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus," and "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." "When the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law," and the Spirit cries out, "Abba, Father!"
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. "Sons" here includes the women, since heirs in the Roman world were sons and Paul says all believers share that standing.

t: Paul's first visit, and his plea
s: Paul says, "You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you." They "welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself." Now he asks, "Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?" and calls them "My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you."
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. Paul does not say what the illness was, and guesses include an eye problem (compare 4:15 and 6:11), malaria and epilepsy. Acts 14:1-20 tells of his work in the south Galatian cities, and Acts 16:6 and 18:23 mention Galatia again.

t: Hagar and Sarah
s: Paul says Abraham "had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman." He says "the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar." The other is "the Jerusalem above," who "is free, and she is our mother." He quotes Isaiah 54:1 and Genesis 21:10.
n: Paul calls this an illustration (4:24), and the Greek word is the root of "allegory." Hagar was an Egyptian slave woman (Genesis 16), and Paul says Mount Sinai is "in Arabia" (4:25). The pin is a background pin, and the exact location of Sinai is uncertain.

t: Stand firm in freedom
s: Paul writes, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery." He warns that if they are circumcised, "Christ will be of no value to you at all." "All that matters is faith, expressed through love." He says "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough."
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. The "yoke of slavery" is the law as a way to be right with God. Paul's harsh wish in 5:12 is aimed at the teachers who pressed circumcision.

t: Walk by the Spirit
s: Paul says "serve one another in love," because "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'" "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." He lists "the acts of the flesh" and then "the fruit of the Spirit": "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control."
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. Lists of vices and virtues were common in Greek and Jewish writing. Paul says "fruit" in the singular, as one harvest.

t: Carry one another's burdens
s: Paul says, "if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness." "Carry one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ." "Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return."
n: Where in Galatia the churches stood is debated. Some scholars place them in the south (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, visited in Acts 13-14), and others in the north around Ancyra and Pessinus. The pin marks the region, not a town. In 6:5 "load" is a different Greek word from "burdens" in 6:2. A burden is a heavy weight that can be shared, and a load is often explained as a pack or cargo each person carries.

t: "The marks of Jesus"
s: Paul says, "See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!" He boasts only "in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," and says "What counts is a new creation." He ends, "let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus."
n: Letters were usually dictated, and the author added a line in his own hand at the end. "Large letters" may be for emphasis or because of poor eyesight. "The marks of Jesus" are most often read as scars from beatings. The pin at Lystra marks the stoning (Acts 14:19), and is a judgment call, since Paul names no place.

t: To God's people in Ephesus
s: Paul writes, "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Paul spent about three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:10; 20:31), and it was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia. Acts 18:19-21 tells of a short first visit, and Acts 19:1-20 of the long stay.

t: "Ever since I heard about your faith"
s: Paul says, "ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, I have not stopped giving thanks for you." He prays that they may know "the hope of His calling" and "the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe," the power God used when "He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Paul had lived among the Ephesians for years, so "ever since I heard" has led some scholars to think the letter went to churches he did not know, and others to think it only means news since he left.

t: Dead in the world of Artemis
s: Paul tells them "you were dead in your trespasses and sins," walking "in the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air." Then, "because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ." "It is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works."
n: Ephesians does not mention Artemis. The pin marks the great temple of Artemis, a wonder of the ancient world and the center of the city's religion (Acts 19:27). Ephesus was known for magic and spirit powers (Acts 19:13-19), which may be the background to "the power of the air" in 2:2. The pin is a judgment call.

t: The dividing wall
s: Paul tells Gentile readers that they were "separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel." "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ. For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility." They are "fellow citizens with the saints," built with "Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone."
n: The Jerusalem Temple had a stone barrier, with Greek and Latin warning notices, that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts on pain of death (Josephus, War 5.193-194). Two of the Greek notices have been found. Acts 21:27-29 tells how Paul was seized after a rumor that he had brought a Gentile into the Temple. Many scholars think Paul has this barrier in mind, and others read "the dividing wall" as the law itself. Paul was in prison because of it.

t: Paul, the prisoner for the Gentiles
s: Paul writes, "I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles." The mystery is "that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus." He prays that they may "comprehend the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ," and ends with praise to the One "who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. The usual view is Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62), where he lived under guard in rented rooms. Caesarea (Acts 23-26) and Ephesus are also suggested, and a few scholars think a follower wrote the letter after Paul's death. The pin at Rome is a judgment call.

t: A letter for many churches?
s: The letter ends, "Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything." Paul had also written to nearby Colossae and told them, "see that you also read the letter from Laodicea" (Colossians 4:16).
