n: Some scholars think "the letter from Laodicea" was this letter, sent around the churches of the Lycus valley with the words "in Ephesus" added in some copies and left out in others. Tychicus is named as the messenger in both letters (Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-9). The pin is a background guess, and the letter's first readers are not known for sure.

t: "He ascended on high"
s: Paul writes, "to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ." He quotes the psalm: "When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men." Then he asks, "What does 'He ascended' mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth?"
n: The quotation is from Psalm 68:18, adapted. The psalm speaks of a victor who receives gifts, and Paul says he gives them. Acts 1:9-12 tells of the ascension from the Mount of Olives. "The lower parts of the earth" may mean the earth itself, or the grave, and scholars disagree. The pin is a judgment call, since Paul does not name a place.

t: Shepherds and teachers for the church
s: Paul says Christ "gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ." They will no longer be "tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching." They are to be "speaking the truth in love."
n: Acts 20:17-38 tells how Paul called the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and charged them to "Be shepherds of the church of God" and to watch for wolves. The pin is Miletus, about 30 miles south of Ephesus. It is a judgment call, and Ephesians itself names no place.

t: Put off the old self
s: Paul says, "you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking." They were taught "to put off your former way of life, your old self," "to be renewed in the spirit of your minds," and "to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness." He adds, "Be angry, yet do not sin," and "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Acts 19:18-20 tells how many Ephesian believers burned their magic books after a failed exorcism by the sons of Sceva. Paul uses the picture of changing clothes, and the same picture is in Colossians 3:9-10.

t: Children of light
s: Paul says, "Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering." "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light." He quotes a saying: "Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. The saying in 5:14 does not match any one Old Testament verse, and it may be a line from an early hymn or baptism song. Isaiah 60:1 is often named as an echo.

t: Filled with the Spirit
s: Paul writes, "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit. Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father." Then, "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Wine and festival drinking were part of the cult life of many Greek cities, and Paul sets singing and thanks in its place. Verse 21 opens the household teaching that follows, and in the Greek the word "submit" is not repeated in 5:22.

t: Christ and the church, husbands and wives
s: Paul says, "Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord," and "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her." Husbands "ought to love their wives as their own bodies." He quotes Genesis 2:24 and says, "This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Greek and Roman writers also wrote about the household, and they spoke mostly to the man as ruler. Paul speaks to wives, husbands, children, parents, slaves and masters in turn, and asks the husband to love and give himself up, which was not the usual advice.

t: Children, slaves and masters
s: Paul says, "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right," and "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath." To slaves, "obey your earthly masters." To masters, "do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him."
n: Colossians 3:18-4:1 has almost the same household teaching, and Colossae is where the slave Onesimus lived (Philemon). Tychicus took Onesimus with him (Colossians 4:7-9). The pin is a judgment call for a letter that may have gone to several churches. Slavery was common in the Roman world, and Paul does not command its end here, but he tells masters they answer to the same Master.

t: The armor of God
s: Paul writes, "Be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. Put on the full armor of God." "For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world's darkness." He names "the belt of truth," "the breastplate of righteousness," the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." He asks them to pray for him, "an ambassador in chains."
n: Acts 28:16 says Paul was kept under a Roman soldier's guard in Rome, and a chained prisoner would have been near one day after day. The armor is a Roman soldier's kit. Much of the picture also comes from Isaiah 11:5 and 59:17. The pin is a judgment call.

t: Tychicus brings the letter
s: Paul writes, "Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts." He ends, "Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love."
n: Some old manuscripts of 1:1 lack "in Ephesus," and many scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. The pin is Ephesus, the city the text names. Tychicus came from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4) and was later sent by Paul to Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:12), and Paul planned to send him to Crete (Titus 3:12). Letters were carried by trusted friends who could read them aloud and answer questions.

t: To all the saints at Philippi
s: Paul writes, "Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." He thanks God "every time I remember you," prays with joy because of their "partnership in the gospel from the first day until now," and is "confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus."
n: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia (Acts 16:12), and the church there was the first Paul founded in Europe, on his second journey (Acts 16:11-40). The first converts named in Acts are Lydia and her household and the jailer and his household. This is the only letter of Paul whose greeting names "overseers and deacons."

t: "My chains have advanced the gospel"
s: Paul writes, "my circumstances have actually served to advance the gospel," because "it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ." Most of the brothers "now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear." Some preach "out of envy and rivalry," but Paul says, "in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. The "palace guard" (Greek praitorion) and "the household of Caesar" (4:22) fit Rome. Paul also says elsewhere that he had been in prison often (2 Corinthians 11:23), and the journeys between Paul and Philippi that the letter implies (2:25-30; 4:18) seem to some readers to suit a nearer city.

t: "To live is Christ"
s: Paul says, "For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain." He is "torn between the two": "I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body." He expects that "Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. Paul does not know how his case will end (1:22), yet he is convinced he will remain and see them again (1:25). A prisoner awaiting trial under Roman guard could be set free or executed.

t: "Worthy of the gospel"
s: Paul writes, "conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ," so that he will know "you stand firm in one spirit, contending side by side for the faith of the gospel, without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you." He adds, "it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him."
n: The Greek for "conduct yourselves" (politeuesthe) means to live as citizens, a word that would stand out in a Roman colony. The letter does not say who the opponents were. "The same struggle you saw I had" points back to Paul's time in Philippi, when the town's magistrates had him beaten and jailed (Acts 16:19-40).

t: The mind of Christ
s: Paul asks them to be "united in spirit and purpose," to do "nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride," but "in humility consider others more important than yourselves." He points to Christ Jesus, "existing in the form of God," who "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant," and "became obedient to death," even "death on a cross." So "God exalted Him to the highest place," and "every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."
n: Many scholars think 2:6-11 is an early hymn or poem that Paul quotes or shapes, and others think he wrote it for this letter. Verses 10-11 echo Isaiah 45:22-23. Roman writers such as Cicero called crucifixion a cruel and shameful penalty. Philippi was a colony where rank and honor mattered, so a hymn that moves from the lowest place to the highest name would be noticed. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: "Shine as lights in the world"
s: Paul writes, "continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose." He says, "Do everything without complaining or arguing," so that "you shine as lights in the world as you hold forth the word of life." His own life may be "poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith," and he is glad.
n: "Complaining or arguing" recalls Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-8; Numbers 14:27), and "a crooked and perverse generation" (2:15) echoes Deuteronomy 32:5. A drink offering was wine poured out beside a sacrifice (Numbers 15:1-10). The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: Timothy, who genuinely cares
s: Paul says, "I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon," and, "I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs." "As a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel." He will send him "as soon as I see what happens with me," and adds, "I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon."
n: Timothy is named with Paul in 1:1. He had joined Paul at Lystra before the trip to Philippi (Acts 16:1-3) and later traveled through Macedonia for him (Acts 19:22). The letter does not say where Timothy was. The pin is the place he was to be sent.

t: Epaphroditus, nearly dead
s: Paul sends back Epaphroditus, "my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs." "He was sick indeed, nearly unto death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me." The church is to "welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor men like him."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. Epaphroditus brought the church's gift (4:18) and most likely carried this letter home. Epaphras, who is named in Colossians 1:7 and 4:12, is probably a different man, though the names are related.

t: "Watch out for those dogs"
s: Paul writes, "Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh!" and then, "it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh."
n: Paul does not name these people. Many think they were Jewish teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised, as in Galatians 5:2-12, and others think they were not believers at all. "Mutilators" (katatome) is a pun on "circumcision" (peritome). Jews sometimes called Gentiles "dogs," and here Paul turns the insult around. The pin is the church that Paul is warning.

t: "I have more": Paul's credentials
s: Paul says he could have confidence in the flesh: "circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless."
n: The letter gives no place. Acts says Paul was brought up in Jerusalem and trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and that he persecuted the church there (Acts 8:1-3; 26:9-11). He was born in Tarsus (Acts 21:39). The pin at Jerusalem is a judgment call. Circumcision on the eighth day is the command of Genesis 17:12 and Leviticus 12:3.

t: "I count all things as loss"
s: Paul says, "whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ." "I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord." He wants "to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings," and says, "I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me."
n: The letter does not name Damascus. Acts 9:1-19 (also 22:6-16 and 26:12-18) tells how Christ stopped Paul on the road to Damascus, and many readers hear "took hold of me" there. The pin is a judgment call. The word translated "rubbish" (skybala) was coarse language for garbage or dung.

t: "Straining toward what is ahead"
s: Paul writes, "Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus."
n: The picture is a runner. Greek cities held athletic contests, and Paul uses a race elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Galatians 2:2). The letter names no track. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: "Our citizenship is in heaven"
s: Paul writes, "Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ." "But our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body."
n: Philippi was a Roman colony settled with army veterans, and its settlers were Roman citizens (Acts 16:12, 21). The Greek word for "citizenship" (politeuma) can also mean a commonwealth or colony. "Savior" and "Lord" were used of emperors in some inscriptions of the Greek East.

t: Euodia and Syntyche
s: Paul writes, "I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord." He asks his "true yokefellow" to "help these women who have labored with me for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life."
n: Nothing else is known of the two women, of Clement, or of the "yokefellow." Some think "yokefellow" is a name (Syzygus), and the letter does not say. Some later writers identified this Clement with Clement of Rome, but the name was very common. Acts 16:13-15 tells of women who gathered to pray at Philippi.

t: "Rejoice in the Lord always"
s: Paul writes, "Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!" "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." He lists "whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable."
n: The Greek for "guard" (phroureo) is a military word. Paul uses it for the guard set on the city of Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32). A Roman colony would have known soldiers on watch. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: Help sent to Thessalonica
s: Paul writes, "as you Philippians know, in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving. For even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again."
n: Acts 17:1-9 tells of Paul in Thessalonica, about 120 km (75 miles) from Philippi in a straight line, along the Egnatian Way. Acts mentions three Sabbaths there. In 1 Thessalonians 2:9 Paul says he worked night and day so as not to burden anyone, so the stay may have lasted longer, or the gifts may have followed him. Paul also says that "brothers" from Macedonia supplied his needs in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:9). "Giving and receiving" is a bookkeeping phrase.

t: The gift brought by Epaphroditus
s: Paul says, "I rejoice greatly in the Lord that at last you have revived your concern for me," and, "I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances." "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." Of their gifts he says, "They are a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God," and "my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. This gift seems to be the reason the letter was written, though Paul saves his thanks until the end. He uses the language of accounts ("credited to your account," 4:17). "Fragrant offering" is the language of sacrifice (Leviticus 1:9).

t: Greetings from Caesar's household
s: Paul ends, "Greet all the saints in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me send you greetings. All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. "The household of Caesar" means the emperor's slaves and freed people, who worked in the palace and in offices across the empire, and inscriptions mention them in many provincial cities, Ephesus among them. It does not mean the emperor's family.

t: To the saints at Colossae
s: Paul writes, "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace and peace to you from God our Father."
n: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley in Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, near the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not founded this church (1:7; 2:1). Timothy is named with him, as in Philippians 1:1. The spot is now a grass-covered mound near the village of Honaz.

t: News from Epaphras
s: Paul writes, "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you, because we have heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints." He speaks of "the faith and love proceeding from the hope stored up for you in heaven" and says, "You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf, and who also informed us of your love in the Spirit."
n: Epaphras is the link between Paul and the Colossians. He comes from the town (4:12) and is with Paul as he writes (4:12; Philemon 23). Acts does not say who started the church. Paul was in Ephesus, roughly 105 miles (170 km) to the west, for two or three years (Acts 19:8-10), and Acts 19:10 says that everyone who lived in the province of Asia heard the word. The letter names faith, hope and love together (1:4-5), as Paul does in 1 Thessalonians 1:3.

t: Prayer for knowledge of His will
s: Paul says, "we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding." The aim is to "walk in a manner worthy of the Lord." He gives thanks that the Father "has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins."
n: The Greek for "redemption" (apolytrosis) belongs to the family of words used for the ransom of slaves and captives. Some readers hear the exodus in the picture of being rescued and brought into another kingdom. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: "The image of the invisible God"
s: Paul writes, "The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities." "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. And He is the head of the body, the church." God "was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross."
n: Many scholars think these verses are an early hymn or poem that Paul quotes or shapes, and others think he composed them for this letter. "Image" echoes Genesis 1:26-27, and "firstborn" (prototokos) can mean the one with the rank of heir, not the first one born, as in Psalm 89:27. The description of Wisdom in Proverbs 8:22-31 and Jewish writings on Wisdom stand behind some of the wording. The list of "thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities" names powers that some in Colossae may have feared.

t: Once alienated, now reconciled
s: Paul says, "Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds. But now He has reconciled you by Christ's physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence." He adds, "if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard."
n: The phrase "Christ's physical body through death" is stressed, and some readers think it answers teachers who played down the body of Christ. "Unblemished" is a word for a sacrifice without defect. Verse 23 says the gospel "has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven," which is a statement of its reach and not a claim that every person had heard it.

t: Paul rejoices in his sufferings
s: Paul writes, "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church." He calls himself its servant and speaks of "the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints," which is "Christ in you, the hope of glory."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. Verse 24 is hard. Christ's sacrifice is complete in this letter (1:20; 2:14), so most readers take the "afflictions" to mean the suffering that comes to the church as it spreads the gospel, which Paul shares. "Mystery" is used here for something once hidden and now made known to the Gentiles.

t: Paul's struggle for Colossae and Laodicea
s: Paul says, "For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me face to face," so that they may know "the mystery of God, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." He adds, "I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric." "Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit."
n: Laodicea was the largest city of the valley and lay about 9 miles (15 km) northwest of Colossae. Paul had not met either church. The Greek word for "struggling" is agon, the word for an athletic contest. The pin at Laodicea shows who else Paul mentions here. Laodicea was rebuilt after the earthquake of about AD 60 without help from Rome, according to the Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 14.27).

t: "See to it that no one takes you captive"
s: Paul writes, "just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him." Then he warns, "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ. For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form."
n: The letter never names the teachers, and scholars still debate what their teaching was. Suggestions include a local Jewish group with visions and rules, a mix of Jewish, pagan and philosophical ideas, and Greek ideas about the "elements" of the world. The Greek word for "takes you captive" (sylagogeo) was used of carrying off plunder or prisoners. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: Buried with Christ, the debt canceled
s: Paul writes, "having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead." God "made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross! And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross."
n: The "debt" (cheirographon) was a handwritten note of debt, the kind of IOU that has survived on papyrus. The picture of "triumphing" is that of a Roman triumph, in which the conquered were led through the streets (see 2 Corinthians 2:14). "Circumcised by Christ and not by human hands" (2:11) is a spiritual circumcision that does not require the Gentile Colossians to receive it in the flesh.

t: "A shadow of the things to come"
s: Paul writes, "let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ." He warns against anyone "who delights in false humility and the worship of angels," and who "has lost connection to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow."
n: Food, feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths are Jewish observances (Numbers 28-29; Leviticus 23). "Worship of angels" may mean worship that angels offer, or worship given to angels. Jews in the valley are known to have kept the festivals: inscriptions of the 2nd and 3rd centuries from Hierapolis mention Unleavened Bread and Pentecost, and a Church council at Laodicea in the 4th century still had to forbid calling on angels. Scholars disagree about what the Colossian teachers actually taught.

t: "Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch"
s: Paul asks, "If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations: 'Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!'?" He says these rules "have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh."
n: Paul quotes slogans of the teachers. The letter does not say what the rules were about. They may have covered food and ritual purity. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: Raised with Christ: seek the things above
s: Paul writes, "since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory."
n: The "right hand of God" is the language of Psalm 110:1. This is where the letter turns from teaching to practice. The Colossians have been raised with Christ (2:12), so they are to live by that. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: Put off the old self, put on the new
s: Paul writes, "Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry." They are to put aside "anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language," since "you have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator. Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all."
n: The picture of taking off and putting on clothes was probably linked to baptism, where converts changed their clothes. "Image of its Creator" returns to Genesis 1:26-27 and to the "image" in 1:15. Scythians were a people north of the Black Sea whom Greeks and Romans thought of as the most wild, so Paul names the lowest place on the Greek scale and includes them. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: "Clothe yourselves": the new community
s: Paul writes, "as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity." "Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs."
n: The phrase "elect of God, holy and beloved" is the language used of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6-8), here given to a mostly Gentile church. Ephesians 5:19 has a very similar line about psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: The Christian household
s: Paul writes, "Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged." To slaves he says, "Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men." "Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven."
n: Greek and Roman writers also gave advice on how to rule a household, but they spoke to the master. Paul addresses the wife, the child and the slave directly, and puts every one of them "in the Lord." Slaves are given the longest section, which suggests many in the church were slaves. A man named Onesimus, a slave, is about to arrive with this letter (4:9; Philemon 10-16). The household instructions in Ephesians 5:22-6:9 are very similar. The pin is the church that Paul is addressing.

t: "A door for the word"
s: Paul writes, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful, as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains. Pray that I may declare it clearly, as I should. Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. Paul asks for prayer for opportunities to speak, not for release. Salt kept food from spoiling and added flavor, so "seasoned with salt" can mean speech that is both pleasant and sound.

t: Tychicus and Onesimus carry the letter
s: Paul writes, "Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts. With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you."
n: Tychicus is also named as the bearer of Ephesians (Ephesians 6:21-22) and appears in Acts 20:4. Onesimus is almost certainly the runaway slave of Philemon (Philemon 10-12), and Philemon seems to have lived at or near Colossae, since Archippus is greeted in both letters (4:17; Philemon 2). The letter does not tell the story, and the pin is the church he is going to.

t: Greetings from Paul's companions
s: Paul writes, "My fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you greetings, as does Mark the cousin of Barnabas. You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him. Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings. These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me." He adds, "Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas send you greetings."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome (Acts 28:16-31, about AD 60-62) is the usual view, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. The pin at Rome is a judgment call. Aristarchus is the Thessalonian who traveled with Paul (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Mark is the John Mark whom Paul had refused to take along (Acts 15:37-39), and the Colossians are told to welcome him. Justus is a common Roman name that this man took alongside the Jewish name Jesus (Joshua). Luke is named as a physician here, and Demas later left Paul (2 Timothy 4:10).

t: Epaphras wrestles in prayer
s: Paul writes, "Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God. For I testify about him that he goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis."
n: Hierapolis lay on a ridge about 12 miles (20 km) from Colossae, across the Lycus from Laodicea, and was known for its hot springs. Colossians 4:13 is the only verse in the New Testament that names the city. Epaphras is with Paul as the letter is written (Philemon 23), so the pin shows the people he is praying for.

t: The letter to be shared with Laodicea
s: Paul writes, "Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house. After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea."
n: Churches met in homes, as they did at Rome, Corinth and Ephesus, and Nympha seems to have been the owner of the house (some manuscripts have the masculine "Nymphas" or "her" for "their"). "The letter from Laodicea" is not known. Some think it is lost, and some think it is Ephesians. Revelation 3:14-22 speaks to this church a generation later.

t: "Complete the ministry": a last word in Paul's hand
s: Paul ends, "Tell Archippus: 'See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.'" "This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. Remember my chains. Grace be with you."
n: Archippus is called Paul's "fellow soldier" in Philemon 2, and some suggest he was a member of Philemon's household, but the letters do not say. The letter does not say what his ministry was. Paul normally used a scribe and then wrote a closing line himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

t: To the church of the Thessalonians
s: Paul writes, "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace and peace to you." He thanks God for "your work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope in our Lord Jesus Christ."
n: Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and lay on the Via Egnatia, the main road from the Adriatic to the Aegean. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts (Acts 15:40; 17:1). Many scholars think this is the earliest letter of Paul that survives, written about AD 50-51, though Galatians may be earlier. The letter names faith, love and hope together, as 1 Corinthians 13:13 does.

t: How the gospel came: "not only in word, but also in power"
s: Paul writes, "our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction." They "became imitators of us and of the Lord," so that "the message of the Lord ring out from you to Macedonia and Achaia." Their story is how they "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God and to await His Son from heaven."
n: Acts 17:1-9 says Paul spoke in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks believed, and a mob attacked the house of Jason. The letter pictures mostly Gentile believers who "turned to God from idols." The city had many cults, among them those of the emperors, so the choice to follow Christ had a cost, and Paul speaks of their "great suffering" (1:6). He may have stayed more than three weeks, but the letter does not say how long.

t: Shameful treatment at Philippi, boldness at Thessalonica
s: Paul reminds them, "we had already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi. But in the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God."
n: Acts 16:19-24 tells how Paul and Silas were dragged before the magistrates at Philippi, beaten with rods and put in the inner prison. Philippi lay about 90 miles (150 km) from Thessalonica by road, along the same Via Egnatia (Acts 17:1). Paul had been a Roman citizen beaten without trial (Acts 16:37), and the "shameful treatment" is a reminder of that. The pin at Philippi marks where it happened.

t: "Gentle among you, like a nursing mother"
s: Paul says, "we never used words of flattery or any pretext for greed. God is our witness!" Then, "we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children. We cared so deeply that we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well."
n: Traveling speakers and teachers of philosophy were common in Greek cities, and some were accused of making money from their audiences. Paul answers charges like these by pointing to what the Thessalonians saw. The Greek word for "nursing mother" (trophos) can mean a nurse who feeds and cares for children. Paul uses the picture of a mother here and of a father in 2:11. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "We worked night and day"
s: Paul writes, "We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God." He treated them "as a father treats his own children—encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory."
n: Paul worked at a trade (Acts 18:3 names tentmaking, or leatherwork) and says the same thing in 2 Thessalonians 3:8. A workshop day started at dawn and might run past dark, so he fitted preaching into the edges of the day. Philippians 4:16 says the Philippians sent help to him in Thessalonica more than once. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: The word of God "now at work in you"
s: Paul thanks God that "when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as the true word of God—the word which is now at work in you who believe." He says they "became imitators of the churches of God in Judea," suffering "from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews."
n: The pin at Jerusalem stands for the churches of Judea that Paul names. Verses 15-16 are some of the hardest in the letter. Paul speaks as a Jew about the Jews who opposed the gospel, in the way the prophets spoke about their own people, and he is not speaking of Jews as a race. Some scholars have thought the passage was added later, but no manuscript is without it, and the question is still debated.

t: "Torn away from you": a longing to return
s: Paul says, "although we were torn away from you for a short time (in person, not in heart), our desire to see you face to face was even more intense. For we wanted to come to you—indeed I, Paul, tried again and again—but Satan obstructed us." He calls them "our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting" at "His coming."
n: The Greek word for "torn away" (aporphanizo) can mean made an orphan. Acts 17:5-10 says Paul and Silas left Thessalonica by night after the riot, when the city officials made Jason and others put up bond. Some scholars think the bond kept Paul from returning, which may be how "Satan obstructed us." The letter does not say. Here the letter first uses the word "coming" (parousia) for the return of Jesus, a word that appears seven times in the two letters.

t: Alone in Athens, Timothy sent back
s: Paul writes, "when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left on our own in Athens. We sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith." He feared "that the tempter had somehow tempted you and caused our labor to be in vain."
n: Acts 17:14-16 says Silas and Timothy stayed in Beroea when Paul was taken on to Athens, and Paul sent for them from there. The letter says Timothy was sent back to Thessalonica from Athens. Acts does not mention this, but Acts 18:5 has them meeting Paul in Corinth. The city had temples, the agora and a long philosophical history (Acts 17:16-34).

t: Timothy returns with good news
s: Paul writes, "Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news about your faith, your love, and the fond memories you have preserved, longing to see us just as we long to see you." He says, "For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was when he wrote. Acts 18:5 has Silas and Timothy joining Paul in Corinth, and 1 Thessalonians 3:6 says Timothy "has returned," so Corinth is the usual view (about AD 50-51). The pin at Corinth follows that clue. The good news is the occasion of the letter. Paul writes the way a man does who has been waiting for news, and the whole letter is warm in tone.

t: A prayer: "May the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love"
s: Paul prays, "Now may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you. And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows, so that He may establish your hearts in blamelessness and holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints."
n: This prayer closes the first half of the letter, which is mostly thanks and memory, and prepares for the instructions that follow. Paul prays to "our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus" together. "With all His saints" can mean the holy ones in general, or the angels, or the believers who have died; the letter does not say. Paul is praying from where he is writing, which the previous stop gives as Corinth.

t: "It is God's will that you should be holy"
s: Paul writes, "we ask and encourage you in the Lord Jesus to live in a way that is pleasing to God." He says, "it is God's will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality; each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God." "For God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness."
n: Greek and Roman society did not hold men to one standard of sexual conduct, and Paul sets a different one for the church. The phrase "control his own body" translates the Greek skeuos, literally "vessel," and scholars disagree whether it means the body or a wife. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: Love, quiet work and daily bread
s: Paul writes, "you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. And you are indeed showing this love to all the brothers throughout Macedonia." He urges them "to aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands, as we instructed you. Then you will behave properly toward outsiders, without being dependent on anyone."
n: Many in a Greek city depended on a patron, a wealthier person who gave help in return for loyalty and public support, and a workman could be tempted to do the same. "Work with your own hands" fits Paul's own example in 2:9. The call to a quiet life prepares for the problem of the idle in 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "Those who sleep in death" and the Lord's coming
s: Paul writes, "we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope." "For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise. After that, we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord." "Therefore encourage one another with these words."
n: Some in the church seem to have been troubled by believers who had died since Paul left, and the letter does not say how many. "Sleep" was a common way to speak of death, and many ancient grave texts show how little hope most people had. The Greek word for "to meet" (apantesis) was used of a group that goes out from a city to greet an important visitor and escort him in, and some scholars see that picture here. Others disagree on how far the picture reaches.

t: "Like a thief in the night": the Day of the Lord
s: Paul writes, "the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, 'Peace and security,' destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman." But "you are all sons of the light and sons of the day." They are to be "putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation." "Therefore encourage and build one another up, just as you are already doing."
n: "The Day of the Lord" comes from the prophets, as in Amos 5:18-20 and Joel 2. Some scholars hear in "Peace and security" an echo of the claims of Roman rule, and others think the words are only general. The armor of faith, love and hope is shorter than the armor in Ephesians 6:13-17, and the images are used differently. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing."
s: Paul writes, "we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction." He urges them "to admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone." "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus. Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good."
n: The church was young and the "leaders" are not named by office. The Greek word for "unruly" (ataktos) was used of soldiers out of rank, and it returns in 2 Thessalonians 3:6-11. The call to "test all things" shows that prophecy was alive in the church and was weighed by the community. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "The One who calls you is faithful": read this letter aloud
s: Paul ends, "may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it." "Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you."
n: The letter does not say where Paul was when he wrote. Acts 18:5 has Silas and Timothy joining Paul in Corinth, and 1 Thessalonians 3:6 says Timothy "has returned," so Corinth is the usual view (about AD 50-51). The pin at Corinth follows that clue. The letter was meant to be heard. Verse 27 orders it read to "all the brothers," and letters in the ancient world were usually read aloud to a group. "Spirit, soul, and body" is not a technical list, and scholars differ on whether Paul meant three parts or one whole person.

t: A second letter to the church of the Thessalonians
s: Paul writes, "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."
n: The greeting is nearly the same as in the first letter. Many readers think it was written only a few months after 1 Thessalonians. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians because of its tone and its sharper view of the end. Others point to the shared names, vocabulary and the handwriting line in 3:17 and hold that he did.

t: "Your faith is growing more and more"
s: Paul writes, "We are obligated to thank God for you all the time, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing more and more, and your love for one another is increasing. That is why we boast among God's churches about your perseverance and faith in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring."
n: The pressure that began at the first visit (Acts 17:5-9) had not ended. The letter does not say what form it took, and it names no persecutors and no events. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven"
s: Paul writes, "it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well. This will take place when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire." Those who reject Him "will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might."
n: The picture draws on the Old Testament, where God appears in fire to judge (Isaiah 66:15) and "repay" echoes Isaiah 66:6. The passage is about relief for the persecuted and not about private revenge, and Romans 12:19 says that vengeance belongs to God. The Greek word for "relief" (anesis) means a loosening, as of a tight bond. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: A prayer: "count you worthy of His calling"
s: Paul prays, "we always pray for you, that our God will count you worthy of His calling, and that He will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith, so that the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ."
n: The prayer ends the thanksgiving. The wording about "worthy" does not say they earn a place, since the call comes by grace (2:13-14). The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: A report that the day has come
s: Paul writes, "we ask you, brothers, not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed by any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us, alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come."
n: Someone in or near the church was saying that the Day of the Lord had arrived, perhaps through a prophecy, a spoken message or a letter said to be from Paul. The letter does not say who. Paul ends the letter with his own handwriting for that reason (3:17). The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "The rebellion" and "the man of lawlessness"
s: Paul writes, "Let no one deceive you in any way, for it will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed. He will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship. So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God."
n: This is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, and readers differ on what and who it means. Some think of an end-time figure, some of a line of rulers, and some of a power at work in history. "Temple of God" may be the Temple in Jerusalem, or the church. The next pin at Jerusalem shows two earlier pictures of the same kind of act.

t: Antiochus and Caligula: the Temple profaned
s: The words about a man who "will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" stand beside earlier events that many readers think of.
n: In 167 BC Antiochus IV set up an altar to Zeus in the Temple (Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:54). In AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself placed in the Temple, and it was never set up because the governor Petronius delayed and Caligula was killed in AD 41. Paul does not name either one. This is a background pin, and Paul does not say that either event is what he means.

t: "You know what is now restraining him"
s: Paul writes, "Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you? And you know what is now restraining him, so that he may be revealed at the proper time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way."
n: The Thessalonians knew what Paul had told them, and the letter does not repeat it. The Greek has "what restrains" (neuter, verse 6) and then "the one who restrains" (masculine, verse 7). Suggestions go from the Roman state to the preaching of the gospel to an angel or to the Holy Spirit, and none of them is certain. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: The lawless one and the Lord's arrival
s: Paul writes, "the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth and annihilate by the majesty of His arrival." His coming brings "every wicked deception directed against those who are perishing, because they refused the love of the truth that would have saved them." "God will send them a powerful delusion so that they believe the lie."
n: "The breath of His mouth" echoes Isaiah 11:4. The Greek for "arrival" is parousia, the same word used for Christ's coming and for the visit of a ruler. Verse 11 says God sends the delusion, and readers differ on whether this is a judgment on those who had already "refused" the truth. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "God has chosen you from the beginning": stand firm
s: Paul writes, "we should always thank God for you, brothers who are loved by the Lord, because God has chosen you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth." "Therefore, brothers, stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter."
n: After the dark picture, Paul turns to what they can be sure of. "Traditions" (paradoseis) are the teachings handed on from one teacher to another, and they are given "by speech or by letter." Some manuscripts read "from the beginning" and others "as firstfruits." The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "Pray for us"
s: Paul writes, "pray for us, that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and be held in honor, just as it was with you. And pray that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men; for not everyone holds to the faith. But the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one."
n: The letter does not say where it was written. Most readers who accept it as Paul's place it in Corinth, a few months after 1 Thessalonians, since Silvanus and Timothy are still with Paul. The pin at Corinth follows that clue. Acts 18:6, 12-17 tells how Paul met opposition in Corinth, and the prayer to be "delivered from wicked and evil men" may refer to it.

t: "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat"
s: Paul writes, "we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition you received from us." He reminds them, "we worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you." "Even while we were with you, we gave you this command: 'If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.'"
n: The "undisciplined" (the same word as "unruly" in 1 Thessalonians 5:14) refers to those who would not work. The letter does not say why. Some think they expected the end very soon, and others think they were relying on wealthy patrons. Paul says he had the right to be paid (3:9; 1 Corinthians 9:4-14) and gave it up as an example. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "Busybodies": work quietly
s: Paul writes, "we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies. We command and urge such people by our Lord Jesus Christ to begin working quietly to earn their own living. But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing." "do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother."
n: The Greek has a wordplay: they are "not working but being busybodies" (ergazomenous, periergazomenous). The aim of the discipline is that the person "may be ashamed," and it is meant to bring him back, as verse 15 says. The pin is the church he is addressing.

t: "This greeting is in my own hand"
s: Paul ends, "may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with all of you. This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you."
n: The letter does not say where it was written. Most readers who accept it as Paul's place it in Corinth, a few months after 1 Thessalonians, since Silvanus and Timothy are still with Paul. The pin at Corinth follows that clue. Paul often used a scribe and then wrote the closing lines himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). Because a letter "seeming to be from us" was already circulating (2:2), this mark mattered.

t: To Timothy, "my true child in the faith"
s: Paul writes, "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there. Paul calls God "our Savior" here and again in 2:3 and 4:10. Timothy had joined Paul at Lystra about AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3) and had been with him in Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus (1 Thessalonians 1:1; Acts 19:22). The greeting adds "mercy" to the usual "grace and peace," as 2 Timothy 1:2 does. The letter says that Paul had gone on to Macedonia and left Timothy at Ephesus (1:3). It does not say where Paul was when he wrote. If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this happened after Acts ends, about AD 62-65, after his time in Rome (Acts 28). Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Every pin here is a judgment call; most stand at Ephesus, where the church is.

t: "Stay on at Ephesus": the false teachers
s: Paul writes, "As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies." He says that "the goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith," and that some "have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk."
n: In Acts 20:29-30 Paul had warned the Ephesian elders that false teachers would rise from among them, and this letter finds that has happened. The letter does not describe the "myths and endless genealogies" fully. Readers have thought of Jewish speculation about the Old Testament family lists, or early forms of the later Gnostic stories, or both. The error is called empty talk because it produces "speculation" and not love. Ephesus was the largest city of the province of Asia, about 105 miles (170 km) from Colossae.

t: "The law is good, if one uses it legitimately"
s: Paul writes, "Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately." The law is for "the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful," and for "anyone else who is averse to sound teaching that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted."
n: The teachers wanted to be "teachers of the law" (1:7). Paul does not attack the law itself. He says it has a proper use against wrongdoing. Many scholars notice that the list in verses 9-10 follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the fifth (killing father or mother) to the ninth (lying). The Greek words for two of the terms ("homosexuals" and "slave traders" in the BSB) are debated in translation. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: "I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor": mercy to Paul
s: Paul writes, "I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy." He then gives the first of the letter's "trustworthy sayings": "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst." He ends with praise: "Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen."
n: Acts 9:1-19 tells how Saul, on the road to Damascus, met the risen Christ. The letter does not name Damascus, so the pin is a judgment call that stands for the change in Paul. The "trustworthy saying" formula occurs five times in the letters to Timothy and Titus (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and nowhere else in Paul. Paul uses his own story as an "example to those who would believe" (1:16).

t: "Fight the good fight": Hymenaeus and Alexander
s: Paul writes, "Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith." He names "Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme."
n: The letter does not say where the "prophecies" about Timothy were spoken (compare 4:14). The pin at Lystra stands for his home (Acts 16:1-2) and is a judgment call. In 1 Corinthians 5:5 Paul uses almost the same words for putting a man out of the church, and the aim there too is that he be saved. Second Timothy 2:17-18 names Hymenaeus as one who taught that the resurrection had already happened. An Alexander in 2 Timothy 4:14 is called a coppersmith who did Paul harm; the letters do not say whether he is the same man, and Acts 19:33 has another Alexander in Ephesus.

t: Prayer for all, and "one mediator"
s: Paul writes, "First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone—for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity." God "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all."
n: Jews prayed for foreign rulers (Jeremiah 29:7), and Josephus says sacrifices were offered at the Temple for the emperor until the revolt of AD 66 (Jewish War 2.409-410). If Paul wrote the letter in the 60s, the emperor was Nero. Ephesus was a center of emperor worship, and the church is told to pray for rulers and not to worship them. The words "one God" echo the great Jewish prayer, "The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: Prayer, dress and women in the assembly
s: Paul writes, "I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension." He asks the women to dress "with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds." He also writes, "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet," and points to Adam and Eve.
n: This is one of the most debated passages in the letters. Some readers take the rule to be lasting, based on the order of creation. Others think it answers a local problem at Ephesus, where false teachers were at work (1:3-7; 2 Timothy 3:6-7) and women in the church may have been drawn to them. The verb for "exercise authority" (authentein) is rare and its sense is argued. Acts 18:26 shows Priscilla helping to teach Apollos at Ephesus, and Romans 16:1 and 16:7 name women who served. "Saved through childbearing" (2:15) has also been read in several ways, among them as a reference to the birth of Christ. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: Overseers: "a noble task"
s: Paul writes, "This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task." The list that follows is mostly about character: "above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach." He "must manage his own household well" and "have a good reputation with outsiders."
n: The Greek word for "overseer" (episkopos) means one who watches over, and in Acts 20:17 and 20:28 and Titus 1:5-7 it is used for the same people as "elders." "The husband of but one wife" has been read as faithful to one wife, as not married again after a wife's death, or as not having divorced and remarried; the church has differed. The household was the center of life in the city, and a church often met in someone's house. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: Deacons and "the women"
s: Paul writes, "Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience." He says, "they must first be tested," and that "those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith."
n: The Greek word for "deacon" (diakonos) means a servant. Phoebe is called one in Romans 16:1 and Paul greets overseers and deacons together in Philippians 1:1. In 3:11 "the women" may mean the wives of deacons or women who were deacons themselves; the Greek can be read either way. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: "The pillar and foundation of the truth": a hymn
s: Paul writes, "Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth." He then quotes what seems to be a hymn: "He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory."
n: The letter names Macedonia (1:3) but no town, so the pin at Philippi is a judgment call for where Paul was. The lines in 3:16 are arranged in pairs, and most scholars think Paul is quoting an early hymn or creed. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and ancient writers describe its many columns (Pliny counts 127), so the image of a "pillar" would have been vivid there.

t: Later times: forbidding marriage and foods
s: Paul writes, "Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons." They "will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving." He answers, "every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected."
n: The letter does not name the group. Some Jewish groups, such as the Essenes, kept to strict rules about food, and some later Christian groups forbade marriage and meat. Paul's answer goes back to Genesis 1:31, where God calls his creation good. "In later times" can mean the time that has already begun, since Paul says the teaching is already at work (4:6-7). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: "Train yourself for godliness"
s: Paul writes, "reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come." He says, "we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe."
n: The Greek verb for "train" (gymnazo) gives us "gymnasium." Greek cities had gymnasia where young men exercised, studied and made connections, and Ephesus had several. Paul uses athletic pictures elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; 2 Timothy 4:7). The saying that God is "Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe" has been read in more than one way, and the first part echoes 2:4. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: "Let no one despise your youth"
s: Paul writes, "Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." He tells Timothy, "devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching," and not to "neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders."
n: If Paul wrote the letter in the 60s, Timothy, who joined Paul about AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3), would probably have been in his thirties or so. The Greek word for "youth" was used loosely of men well into that range, so it is not clear how young he was. Scripture was read aloud in the assembly because few could read, and copies were scarce. Second Timothy 1:6 speaks of the same gift "through the laying on of my hands," so Paul may have been among those who laid hands on him. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: The church as a family: honor widows
s: Paul writes, "Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity." He says, "Honor the widows who are truly widows," and, "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."
n: In Greek and Roman cities a widow without a husband, sons or property had little security, and a family was expected to care for her. Acts 6:1 shows that widows needed help from the first years of the church. The church is pictured as a household with fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters, and the same picture appears in 3:15. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: The list of widows
s: Paul writes, "A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds." He says, "refuse to enroll younger widows," and advises them "to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander." He adds, "If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened."
n: The "list" may be a roll of widows who received the church's help, or a group who served the church in return, or both; the letter does not say. Roman law under Augustus pressed widows to marry again, which fits the advice to younger widows. "Washing the feet of the saints" (5:10) was a servant's work (John 13:5-14). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: Elders, "double honor" and a little wine
s: Paul writes, "Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,' and, 'The worker is worthy of his wages.'" He adds, "Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments."
n: The first saying is Deuteronomy 25:4, which Paul also uses in 1 Corinthians 9:9. The second matches Jesus' words in Luke 10:7. "Double honor" can mean respect and pay. A charge against an elder needs "two or three witnesses," as Deuteronomy 19:15 requires. Ancient doctors often prescribed a little wine for the stomach, and the advice in 5:23 is personal and brief. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: Slaves, and teachers who see godliness "as a means of gain"
s: Paul writes, "All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God's name and our teaching will not be discredited." Those who teach another doctrine have "an unhealthy interest in controversies and semantics," and "regard godliness as a means of gain."
n: Slaves were a large part of the population in cities like Ephesus, and many churches had slaves and masters among their members (Colossians 3:22-4:1; Philemon). Paul does not say here that slavery is right. The advice aims to keep the church from being slandered, and it says that believing masters are "brothers" (6:2). Traveling teachers in the Greek world often charged fees, and the charge of teaching for gain was a familiar one. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: "Godliness with contentment is great gain"
s: Paul writes, "godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these." He warns, "the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows."
n: The Greek has no word for "the" before "root," so it can be read "a root of all kinds of evil," and this is how many translations render it. The saying about bringing nothing into the world is close to Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:15. Ephesus was a rich trading city, and Paul says wealth was one of the teachers' temptations. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: The good confession before Pilate
s: Paul writes, "But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith." He charges Timothy "in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate."
n: John 18:33-37 gives the fullest account of Jesus' answer to Pilate, and the Gospels place the trial in Jerusalem, so the pin stands there. "Man of God" was a name for Moses, Samuel, David and Elijah in the Old Testament. The "good confession" that Timothy made (6:12) may refer to his baptism, his ordination, or a public stand, and the letter does not say which. The doxology that follows calls God "the King of kings and Lord of lords" (6:15). "King of kings" was a title of Persian and Parthian monarchs, and Roman emperors were called "lord" and "savior," so the words would have been heard against the claims of rulers.

t: "Guard what has been entrusted to you"
s: Paul writes, "Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy." He ends, "O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called 'knowledge.' "
n: The Greek for "what has been entrusted" (parathēkē) means a deposit left in someone's care, and 2 Timothy 1:12 and 1:14 use the same word. The word "knowledge" is gnosis in Greek, and later Gnostic groups used it of their secret teaching, but the letter does not say which group it has in mind. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

t: To Timothy, "my beloved child"
s: Paul writes, "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Paul begins with "the promise of life" even as he faces death (4:6). The greeting is almost the same as 1 Timothy 1:2 (there it is "my true child in the faith"); here Timothy is "my beloved child," a warmer note. Timothy had joined Paul at Lystra about AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3). The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier ("like a criminal," 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

t: Tears, and the faith of Lois and Eunice
s: Paul writes, "I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers. Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy." He is "reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well."
