n: Acts 16:1 says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek, and it places the family at Lystra (or nearby Derbe), so the pin there is a judgment call. Lois and Eunice are named only here. The letter does not say what caused the tears; they may come from their last parting. Paul speaks of serving God "as did my forefathers," so he sees his faith as growing out of Israel's, and Timothy's too (3:15). The grandmother, mother and son make three generations, a picture of what Paul asks Timothy to pass on in 2:2.

t: "Fan into flame the gift of God"
s: Paul writes, "For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The Greek verb (anazopyreo) means to stir up a fire again, as one blows on banked coals. The "laying on of my hands" is likely the same event as the laying on of hands "of the elders" in 1 Timothy 4:14, where Paul and the elders acted together; the letters do not explain further. The "spirit of fear" may hint that Timothy was timid, as 1 Corinthians 16:10-11 also suggests, but the letter does not say so directly.

t: "Do not be ashamed" of the testimony or of me
s: Paul writes, "So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God." He says, "I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day." Christ "has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. In the Roman world a prisoner in chains was shameful, and to be linked to one risked your own name. Paul answers with the same word he used in Romans 1:16: "I am not ashamed of the gospel." The phrase "what I have entrusted to Him" can mean what Paul has put in God's keeping (his life, his work) or what God has put in Paul's keeping (the gospel); the Greek word is the same "deposit" found in 1:14 and 1 Timothy 6:20. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier ("like a criminal," 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

t: "Guard the treasure entrusted to you"
s: Paul writes, "Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The word for "pattern" (hypotyposis) means an outline or sketch that a writer or artist follows. The "treasure" is the deposit (parathēke) of 1 Timothy 6:20. A deposit in the ancient world was something valuable left with a trusted person, who had to hand it back unharmed. Timothy is asked to do this "with the help of the Holy Spirit," not alone.

t: Deserted by Asia, refreshed by Onesiphorus
s: Paul writes, "You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Asia was the Roman province whose chief city was Ephesus, so "everyone in the Province of Asia" probably means that those from Asia who had been in Rome did not stand with Paul; the letter does not say how many or why. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named only here. Onesiphorus is also greeted in 4:19, where Paul greets "the household" and not the man himself, and some have thought he had died; that is a guess. He had also helped Paul "in Ephesus" (1:18). A man who "searched diligently" suggests that Paul was not easy to find in a large city.

t: Be strong: soldier, competitor, farmer
s: Paul writes, "You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well." He gives three pictures: "a good soldier of Christ Jesus," a competitor who "does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules," and a farmer who "should be the first to partake of the crops."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Paul's line has four links: Paul, Timothy, "faithful men," and "others as well." The soldier gives up civilian business to please his commander, the competitor keeps the rules, and the farmer works before he eats. Each picture asks for hard effort that will pay later. Paul uses the soldier and the athlete elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:7, 9:24-27; Philippians 2:25).

t: "The word of God cannot be chained!"
s: Paul writes, "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!" He gives a "trustworthy saying": "If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. The word for "criminal" (kakourgos) is the same one Luke uses for the two men crucified with Jesus (Luke 23:32-33). Most scholars think the "trustworthy saying" in 2:11-13 is an early hymn or creed that Paul quotes; it is one of five such sayings in the letters to Timothy and Titus (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). The line "If we deny Him, He will also deny us" echoes Jesus' words in Matthew 10:33.

t: The approved workman; Hymenaeus and Philetus
s: Paul writes, "Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth." The talk of the false teachers "will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The Greek for "accurately handles" (orthotomeo) literally means to cut straight, as a road is cut or a stone is squared; the word is rare and its first picture is debated. Hymenaeus was already named in 1 Timothy 1:20, where Paul said he had handed him over to Satan. Philetus appears only here. The claim that "the resurrection has already occurred" may mean a spiritual rising in baptism, with no future raising of the body; the letter does not explain it. The quotation "The Lord knows those who are His" (2:19) is close to Numbers 16:5, from the story of Korah's revolt.

t: A large house: vessels for honor
s: Paul writes, "A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay." He says, "if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work." Then he writes, "Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace," and says the Lord's servant "must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. A wealthy Roman household kept fine vessels of silver for the table and plain clay ones for common use; the finds from Boscoreale near Pompeii show how much silver a rich house could hold. Paul uses a clay-pot picture elsewhere (Romans 9:21; 2 Corinthians 4:7). Here the "large house" is likely the church, which holds both honorable and common members. The "snare of the devil" (2:26) is a hunting picture of a trap, and the captives may "come to their senses" and be released.

t: The last days: "lovers of themselves"
s: Paul writes, "But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy." The list goes on to people "having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!"
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The list has about eighteen terms, and similar lists appear in Romans 1:29-31 and Galatians 5:19-21. The Bible often calls the whole time since Christ's first coming "the last days" (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and Paul says this is already the case, since he tells Timothy to turn away from such people now. The first term, "lovers of themselves" (philautoi), opens the list, and "lovers of pleasure" and "lovers of God" balance each other near its end.

t: Jannes and Jambres
s: Paul writes, "They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth." He adds, "they will not advance much further."
n: The Old Testament does not name Jannes and Jambres. Exodus 7:11 speaks of the wise men and sorcerers of Pharaoh without naming them. Jewish tradition did name them: the Damascus Document from Qumran mentions Jannes (and his brother) who opposed Moses, the Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus gives both names, and a damaged Greek papyrus of the third century AD preserves part of a "Book of Jannes and Jambres." The pin at Egypt is a judgment call for the story Paul refers to. The "households" and the women (3:6) fit a picture of teachers who worked in private homes, where the early church met. The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call.

t: Antioch, Iconium, Lystra: "observed my teaching"
s: Paul writes, "You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted."
n: These three cities are the places of Paul's first journey (Acts 13:14-14:23). At Pisidian Antioch Jews drove him out (Acts 13:50), at Iconium a plot to stone him forced him to leave (Acts 14:5-6), and at Lystra he was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Timothy was from that region, so he would have known these stories, even if he did not join Paul until a later visit (Acts 16:1-3). The pin at Lystra stands for all three. The Greek word for "imposters" (goetes) can also mean magician or deceiver.

t: "All Scripture is God-breathed"
s: Paul writes, "But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The word "God-breathed" (theopneustos) is found only here in the New Testament. "The Holy Scriptures" Timothy knew from childhood were the Old Testament, which his mother and grandmother would have taught him (1:5); the writings of the apostles were not yet gathered. The line "All Scripture is God-breathed" can also be translated "Every God-breathed Scripture is useful," and Christians have read the verse both ways. Scripture was kept on scrolls and read aloud in the assembly (1 Timothy 4:13).

t: "Preach the word"
s: Paul writes, "I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction." He warns that "the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. A charge "in the presence of God" is solemn, formal language. The "itching ears" (knethomenoi) were ears that wanted to be tickled, and the picture is of people who want teachers to tell them what they like to hear. The noun "evangelist" ("do the work of an evangelist") is rare: it occurs only here, in Acts 21:8 (of Philip) and in Ephesians 4:11.

t: "I have fought the good fight"
s: Paul writes, "For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. "Poured out like a drink offering" uses the same verb (spendomai) as Philippians 2:17, and "departure" (analysis) can mean loosening a ship's ropes or striking a tent, a picture of leaving. The "crown" was a wreath of leaves given to the winner at games such as the Isthmian Games near Corinth (1 Corinthians 9:25). Paul says it will be given by the "righteous Judge," the opposite of an unjust court. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier ("like a criminal," 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

t: Demas, Crescens, Titus, Luke, Mark, Tychicus
s: Paul writes, "Make every effort to come to me quickly, because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Demas was with Paul in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24; here he has left. Some early manuscripts read "Gaul" for "Galatia." Dalmatia is on the Adriatic coast in what is now Croatia and Bosnia, near Illyricum (Romans 15:19). Luke is named as a companion in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24. Mark had been the cause of Paul and Barnabas parting (Acts 15:37-39), and Paul now calls him "useful." Tychicus carried letters in Ephesians 6:21 and Colossians 4:7.

t: The cloak and the scrolls
s: Paul writes, "When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments."
n: Troas was the port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor where Paul had visited several times (Acts 16:8-11; 20:5-12; 2 Corinthians 2:12). Carpus is named only here. The Greek word for the "cloak" (phailones) is rare, and some ancient readers took it as a book-case. The "scrolls" were probably papyrus rolls and the "parchments" (membranai) were of animal skin, perhaps notebooks or copies of Scripture; the letter does not say what they held. The request shows Paul in a cold prison, wanting both warmth and something to read.

t: Alexander the coppersmith
s: Paul writes, "Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Acts 19:33 names an Alexander at the riot in the Ephesus theater, and 1 Timothy 1:20 names one whom Paul "handed over to Satan"; the letter does not say whether any of these is the same man, since Alexander was a common name. The words "The Lord will repay him according to his deeds" echo Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, and they leave justice with God and not with Paul or Timothy.

t: The first defense: "the Lord stood by me"
s: Paul writes, "At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom."
n: The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul's chains, so the pin stands at Rome. The "first defense" (apologia) seems to be a first hearing before the final verdict. A Roman defendant would normally have a patron or advocate to stand beside him, and none came. "The mouth of the lion" echoes Psalm 22:21 and Daniel 6:20-22; it may be a figure for danger or death, or for Nero, and the letter does not say. Paul says he was rescued yet he still expects to die (4:6), and he trusts the Lord to bring him into His heavenly kingdom. The prayer that it "not be charged against them" is close to Stephen's in Acts 7:60.

t: Final greetings: Prisca, Aquila, Erastus, Trophimus
s: Paul writes, "Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all."
n: The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila had lived at Corinth, Ephesus and Rome (Acts 18:2, 18:26; Romans 16:3-5); their greeting here is another sign that Timothy is at Ephesus. Erastus may be the city treasurer of Corinth in Romans 16:23. Trophimus was an Ephesian who came with Paul to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4; 21:29), so leaving him ill at Miletus must have happened on a later trip, which is one reason many place this letter after Acts ends. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.3) names a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, but the letter does not say whether this is the same man. "Before winter" matters because sea travel stopped in winter. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier ("like a criminal," 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

t: To Titus, "my true child"
s: Paul writes, "Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began." He greets "Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The opening is long: four verses before the greeting itself. Paul calls himself "a servant of God," which he does in no other opening; in Romans 1:1 he is "a servant of Christ Jesus." The Greek word for "cannot lie" (apseudes) occurs only here in the New Testament, and Paul will soon quote a Cretan saying that Cretans are "always liars" (1:12). The word "Savior" is used three times of God and three times of Christ in this short letter (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6). Titus does not say where Paul was when he wrote, but 3:12 says he plans to spend the winter at Nicopolis. If Paul wrote the letter, the usual view is that it comes after Acts ends, about AD 62-65, and that Paul and Titus had worked together on Crete (1:5); Acts does not tell that visit. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Titus is known from other letters: a Greek who was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3) and Paul's trusted envoy to Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6-7; 8:16-17).

t: Left in Crete to set things in order
s: Paul writes, "The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Acts 27:7-13 shows Paul sailing past Crete as a prisoner, but Acts does not say he taught there, so the work behind Titus 1:5 is usually placed after Acts. Cretans were among the listeners at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and the Jewish writer Philo lists Crete among the places where Jews lived (Embassy to Gaius 282), so a first seed may have come through such travelers. The verb for "set in order" (epidiorthoo) occurs only here in the New Testament. Paul and Barnabas had likewise appointed elders in each church on the first journey (Acts 14:23). The letter says "in every town," so the churches were probably small groups in many places across the island.

t: The elder: blameless, a steward of God
s: Paul writes, "An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. As God's steward, an overseer must be above reproach." He must be "hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined," and "must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. "Elder" and "overseer" name the same person here, as in Acts 20:17 and 20:28. The list is close to the one in 1 Timothy 3:1-7, but not identical: Titus has no ban on a recent convert, and it puts the weight on holding to the faithful word and answering opponents. "The husband of but one wife" is debated as it is in 1 Timothy 3:2: it may mean faithful to one wife, no polygamy, or not remarried after a divorce or a wife's death. The Greek for "believers" in "children who are believers" can also mean "faithful," and translators differ. A "steward" (oikonomos) managed a household for its owner, and Paul says the overseer manages God's household.

t: Rebellious talkers who upset households
s: Paul writes, "For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. "Those of the circumcision" most likely means Jewish believers who pressed circumcision and the law on Gentile believers, as in Acts 11:2, Acts 15:1 and Galatians 2:12. The letter does not spell out what they taught; the clues are "Jewish myths" (1:14), questions about purity (1:15) and "quarrels about the law" (3:9). The Greek for "must be silenced" (epistomizo) is a rare word that means to stop the mouth, as one muzzles an animal. The harm is to "entire households," and early churches met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Love of "dishonorable gain" is also charged against false teachers in 1 Timothy 6:5.

t: "Cretans are always liars": the poet
s: Paul writes, "As one of their own prophets has said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.' This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth."
n: The pin stands at Knossos as a judgment call. The letter does not name the poet. Later Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria and Jerome name Epimenides, a poet and seer traditionally from Knossos and placed by later writers about 600 BC. The first words of the line, "Cretans are always liars," also open a verse of Callimachus' Hymn to Zeus (3rd century BC), and Greek writers often joked about Cretan lying. Paul calls the poet "one of their own prophets," which here means a seer or poet, not an Old Testament prophet. He says the saying is true of the people he has in mind, but the "rebuke" is aimed at the teachers of 1:10-11 and is meant to restore them to "sound" faith. The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there.

t: To the pure all things are pure
s: Paul writes, "To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The saying echoes teaching about clean and unclean food: Jesus said that what goes into a person does not defile him (Mark 7:14-23), and Paul wrote that nothing is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14, 20). It is not a claim that anything is allowed. The point is that the rules the teachers press (1:14) cannot cleanse a person whose mind and conscience are defiled, and the proof is how they live. The same contrast between profession and "actions" appears in 2 Timothy 3:5.

t: Sound teaching for older men and women
s: Paul writes, "But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine. Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good." They can "train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The Greek for "sound" (hygiaino) means healthy, the root of our word "hygiene," and the pastoral letters use it again and again for teaching that is healthy (1 Timothy 1:10; 6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 1:9, 13). The word for "teachers of good" (kalodidaskalos) occurs only here. Lists of duties for each group in a household, such as Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:22-6:9 and 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, were common in the ancient world, and Paul gives the reason as the reputation of the gospel: "so that the word of God will not be discredited." Readers differ on how "submissive to their own husbands" applies today; the same word is used of all believers toward one another in Ephesians 5:21.

t: Younger men, and Titus as an example
s: Paul writes, "In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Younger men get only one request, to be self-controlled, a word that runs through the chapter (2:2, 5, 6, 12). Titus is told to be "an example," as Timothy is told in 1 Timothy 4:12. The Greek word for "wholesome" (hygies) is the same "healthy" word used for sound teaching. The "opponents" are outsiders, and the aim is that they find nothing bad to say, which echoes the concern for reputation in 2:5 and 2:10.

t: Slaves who adorn the teaching
s: Paul writes, "Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Slaves were part of most Roman households. The Greek verb for "stealing" (nosphizomai) means to keep something back for oneself, and it is the verb used in Acts 5:2-3 of Ananias and Sapphira. The word "adorn" (kosmeo) is the word for dressing or decorating, so even a slave's honest conduct can make the gospel attractive. Paul does not say here whether slavery is right; 1 Timothy 1:10 lists slave traders among the lawless, and Philemon 15-16 asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother. Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1 give duties to masters, which Titus does not.

t: "The grace of God has appeared"
s: Paul writes, "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. "Appeared" (epiphaino) and "appearance" (epiphaneia) are words for the arrival of a god or a ruler, and Paul uses the second word for both comings of Christ (2 Timothy 1:10; 4:1, 8). Grace here "instructs" (paideuo), the word for training a child, so grace teaches by discipline as well as by pardon. Most scholars read "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" as one person, so that Jesus is called God; others read two persons, the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. The Greek grammar allows both, and the debate is an old one (compare 2 Peter 1:1). The phrase "a people for His own possession" recalls Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 14:2, and "redeem us from all lawlessness" echoes Psalm 130:8.

t: Speak with authority; submit to rulers
s: Paul writes, "Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you." He continues, "Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Crete was a Roman province, joined with Cyrene as one province, and Rome had taken the island only after a hard war in 69-67 BC, so a reminder about rulers was not empty. Paul gives the same advice in Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Timothy 2:1-2, as does Peter in 1 Peter 2:13-17. "Let no one despise you" is the same line given to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:12. The aim is again outward: believers are to be "peaceable and gentle" to everyone, so that outsiders see good, not trouble.

t: Washed and renewed: the kindness of God appeared
s: Paul writes, "For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The passage names God our Savior, the Holy Spirit and Jesus Christ our Savior, and some scholars think verses 4-7 are an early hymn or baptismal creed that Paul quotes. "His love for mankind" is one word (philanthropia), used of kind rulers in Greek writing and here of God. "Washing of new birth" is often read as baptism (compare Acts 22:16 and Ephesians 5:26), but whether baptism is meant, or only the cleansing work of the Spirit, is debated. The Greek for "new birth" (palingenesia) is used in Matthew 19:28 for the renewal of all things. "Poured out" recalls Joel 2:28-29 and Acts 2:17, 33, and salvation "not by the righteous deeds we had done" matches Ephesians 2:8-9.

t: Good deeds, foolish controversies and the divisive man
s: Paul writes, "This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people. But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless. Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. "This saying is trustworthy" is one of five such sayings in the letters to Timothy and Titus (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and scholars debate whether it points back to 3:4-7 or forward to the call to good deeds. The "divisive man" is a hairetikos, the word that gave us "heretic," but here it means someone who causes factions, and the later sense of a condemned heretic had not yet formed. The "first and second admonition" means two warnings, then he is to be left alone; compare Matthew 18:15-17. "Self-condemned" (autokatakritos) occurs only here, and it says that by refusing correction he has judged himself. The "genealogies" and "quarrels about the law" recall 1:14 and 1 Timothy 1:4.

t: Artemas or Tychicus; winter at Nicopolis
s: Paul writes, "As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there."
n: The pin is a judgment call. Several cities were named Nicopolis (the name means City of Victory), and the letter does not say which one Paul meant. Most scholars think of Nicopolis in Epirus, on the Ionian coast of Greece, which Augustus founded after his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Paul had preached as far as Illyricum (Romans 15:19), which lies north of Epirus, and 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus later went to Dalmatia, part of Illyricum. Artemas is named only here. Tychicus appears in Acts 20:4, Ephesians 6:21-22, Colossians 4:7-8 and 2 Timothy 4:12. Whichever man came would take over on Crete. Winter is mentioned because sea travel was dangerous in that season, as Acts 27:9-12 shows off the coast of Crete itself. Titus does not say where Paul was when he wrote, but 3:12 says he plans to spend the winter at Nicopolis. If Paul wrote the letter, the usual view is that it comes after Acts ends, about AD 62-65, and that Paul and Titus had worked together on Crete (1:5); Acts does not tell that visit. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul's name. Titus is known from other letters: a Greek who was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3) and Paul's trusted envoy to Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6-7; 8:16-17).

t: Zenas the lawyer and Apollos
s: Paul writes, "Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need. And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful. All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you."
n: The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Zenas is named only here. In the rest of the New Testament the word "lawyer" (nomikos) means an expert in the law of Moses (Luke 7:30; 10:25), so he may have been a Jewish believer trained in Scripture, but the letter does not say. Apollos was a Jew from Alexandria who taught at Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24-28; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4-6; 16:12). The verb "equip" (propempo) means to send someone on his way with supplies and, often, an escort (Romans 15:24; 1 Corinthians 16:6; 3 John 6). The two men were probably passing through Crete, and some think they carried the letter, but that is a guess. The "pressing needs" are practical needs like these, and Paul wants believers to meet them so that they are not "unfruitful." The greeting from "all who are with me" does not name anyone.

t: Paul and Timothy to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the house church
s: Paul writes, "Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul does not call himself an apostle here, as he does in most letters; he calls himself a prisoner, which sets the tone of an appeal. Timothy joins him as sender, as in Colossians 1:1 and Philippians 1:1. "Fellow worker" is the word Paul uses for Titus, Timothy, Mark, Luke and others. Apphia is probably Philemon's wife and Archippus perhaps his son, but the letter says only "sister" and "fellow soldier," and Colossians 4:17 tells Archippus to complete the ministry he received. Churches met in houses (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15). Verses 4 to 21 say "you" in the singular, while verses 3, 22 and 25 use the plural, so the letter was meant to be read aloud to the whole church.

t: Thanks for Philemon's faith and love
s: Paul writes, "I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." He prays that Philemon's "partnership in the faith may become effective" and says, "I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. The thanks follows the pattern of Greek letters, which often began with a prayer or thanks to the gods for the person written to. The word for "partnership" (koinonia) can also mean sharing or fellowship, and it returns in verse 17 when Paul says, "if you consider me a partner." The Greek word for "hearts" in verse 7 (splagchna) means the inner organs, the seat of feeling; Paul uses it again in verses 12 and 20. Philemon has already shown that he refreshes others, which is what Paul will soon ask him to do for Onesimus and for Paul himself.

t: I prefer to appeal on the basis of love
s: Paul writes, "So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well."
n: The letter does not name Paul's prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul's two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul's hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Paul says he could give an order but will not. The Greek word translated "aged" (presbytes) can also be read as the similar word presbeutes, "ambassador," and Paul calls himself an ambassador in Ephesians 6:20 and 2 Corinthians 5:20; some scholars prefer that reading, but the manuscripts support "aged." Paul calls himself a prisoner again, and the weight of his chains is part of the appeal.

t: Onesimus: once useless, now useful
s: Paul writes, "I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. I am sending back to you him who is my very heart."
n: The letter does not name Paul's prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul's two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul's hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Onesimus is the first name in the request, held back until verse 10. The name means "useful" or "profitable" and was a common name for slaves. Paul plays on it: "useless" (achrestos) and "useful" (euchrestos) are close in sound to "Christ" (Christos), which some scholars think Greek speakers could hear as chrestos, "good." Paul says he became Onesimus's "father" in chains, so Onesimus met him in prison and believed there. The usual view is that Onesimus was a slave who had run away. Some scholars suggest he came to Paul as a slave in trouble who sought a friend of his master to speak for him, but the letter does not say how he reached Paul.

t: Sent back, not kept: nothing without your consent
s: Paul writes, "I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will."
n: The letter does not name Paul's prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul's two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul's hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Paul admits that he would have liked to keep Onesimus and says he will not do so without Philemon's agreement. Under Roman law a slave belonged to his owner, and anyone who kept a runaway could be accused of theft. Paul stays on the right side of that law, yet leaves the real decision with Philemon. The "consent" (gnome) is Philemon's own judgment, and the word "free will" (hekousion) is the opposite of being forced.

t: No longer a slave, but a beloved brother
s: Paul writes, "For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good—no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul says "perhaps" and uses a passive verb, "was separated," which leaves God as the unnamed actor. "For good" translates a word that can mean forever. The letter does not say outright that Philemon should free Onesimus. Readers differ: some think Paul hints at freedom, some think he asks Philemon to accept Onesimus as a brother while he remains a slave, and others think he leaves it open. Paul says Onesimus is a brother "both in person and in the Lord," which means both as a person in the household and as a believer.

t: Receive him as you would receive me
s: Paul writes, "So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. The language is that of business. "Charge it to my account" (ellogeo) is a ledger term. Paul writes the promise in his own hand, which made it a signed note; he usually dictated and then added a closing line himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). "You owe me your very self" suggests that Paul had a part in Philemon's own conversion, but the letter does not say where. Paul had not visited Colossae (Colossians 2:1). If Philemon met Paul at Ephesus, as some suggest, he would have been one of the many who heard the word there (Acts 19:10). Paul does not say what Onesimus had done wrong or owed, and "wronged" and "owes" are both stated as an "if."

t: Refresh my heart: you will do even more
s: Paul writes, "Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. "Let me have some benefit" is the verb oninemi, from the same root as the name Onesimus, so Paul puns once more. "Refresh my heart" repeats the words of verse 7, where Philemon is said to have refreshed the hearts of the saints. "Even more than I ask" has led some readers to think Paul hopes for Onesimus's freedom, while others think he means a warmer welcome than Philemon might have thought of. The letter does not say.

t: Prepare a guest room for me
s: Paul writes, "In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you."
n: The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called "one of you" in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul expects to be set free and to visit. The word "guest room" (xenia) means lodging for a guest. Paul tells the Philippians of a similar hope (Philippians 2:24), and in Romans 15:23-24 he looks toward Spain from Rome, so which hope applies depends on where he was imprisoned. A visit to Colossae would be a good fit if he were in Ephesus or Caesarea, and a harder one if he were in Rome. The "your" in "your prayers" is plural, so he is also speaking to the church.

t: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke send greetings
s: Paul writes, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit."
n: The letter does not name Paul's prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul's two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul's hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Epaphras is from Colossae (Colossians 4:12) and brought the report of the church to Paul (Colossians 1:7-8). Here he is called Paul's "fellow prisoner"; in Colossians 4:10 that word is used for Aristarchus. Mark is the John Mark of Acts 12:12 and 15:37-39, who had left Paul on the first journey. Demas later left Paul (2 Timothy 4:10). Luke is Paul's companion in the "we" sections of Acts. The last word of the letter, "your spirit," is plural in Greek, so the whole church is blessed.

t: God has spoken to us by his Son
s: The writer says, "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe. The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word. After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The opening is one long Greek sentence. It sets the Son beside the prophets, who spoke "in many different ways," and calls him heir of all things, the one through whom the universe was made, and the one who sits at the right hand after purifying sins. The letter does not open with a name or a greeting, unlike the letters of Paul, and it ends like a letter, so many call it a sermon with a letter's ending.

t: The Son is greater than the angels
s: The writer says, "For to which of the angels did God ever say: "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father"? Or again: "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son"? And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: "Let all God's angels worship Him.""
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer strings together quotations from the Psalms, 2 Samuel and Deuteronomy to show that the Son is called Son in a way angels never are. The quotations follow the Greek Old Testament, which differs in some words from the Hebrew text, and the Dead Sea Scrolls show that Jews of the time thought a good deal about angels.

t: Pay closer attention: do not drift away
s: The writer says, "We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,"
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). This is the first of five warnings (2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 5:11-6:12; 10:26-39; 12:25-29). The argument runs from lesser to greater: if the message spoken through angels (the law) had force, how much more the one spoken by the Lord. Jewish tradition said that angels were present when the law was given (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19).

t: Made like us: crowned with glory through suffering
s: The writer says, "Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem, where the Gospels place Jesus' suffering and death, though this passage names no place. The writer quotes Psalm 8 and says Jesus shared "flesh and blood" in order to free those held in slavery by the fear of death. Verse 17 introduces the word "high priest" for the first time, and the idea comes back in 4:14-5:10 and chapters 7-10.

t: Greater than Moses; Today, if you hear his voice
s: The writer says, "Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness,"
n: The pin stands at Kadesh-barnea, the oasis in the Negev where Israel refused to enter the land (Numbers 13-14), which is the best-known candidate for the rebellion the writer quotes from Psalm 95. The letter itself does not name the place. The identification of Kadesh with Ain el-Qudeirat is widely accepted but not certain. Moses is faithful as a servant in God's house, the Son as the builder and the Son over the house (3:5-6). The "rest" the people failed to enter (3:11, 18; 4:1-11) is the central image of this section.

t: A great high priest who sympathizes
s: The writer says, "During the days of Jesus' earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence. Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered."
n: The pin stands at Gethsemane, the place the Gospels give for Jesus' prayer with "loud cries and tears." The letter does not name the garden, and the words may also gather up other moments of his prayer. Hebrews says the high priest must be taken from among men, must be called by God as Aaron was, and can "deal gently" with the ignorant because he is himself subject to weakness. The same verse (5:6) quotes Psalm 110:4 and calls Jesus a priest "in the order of Melchizedek."

t: Press on to maturity: the anchor of the soul
s: The writer says, "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The section begins with a rebuke that the readers need milk and not solid food, and moves through the hardest passage in the letter (6:4-8) to the promise God made to Abraham with an oath (6:13-18). Readers differ widely on whether 6:4-6 describes believers who lose their salvation or people who only seemed to share in it; the letter itself says it is "convinced of better things" for its readers (6:9). The "anchor" is a harbor image; Hebrews 6:19 is the only place in the New Testament that uses an anchor as a picture of hope.

t: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High
s: The writer says, "This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything. First, his name means "king of righteousness." Then also, "king of Salem" means "king of peace." Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem, which Psalm 76:2 and many readers identify with Salem; Genesis 14 does not say where Salem was. The writer draws on only two Old Testament passages, Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110:4. The Dead Sea Scrolls (11Q13) also treat Melchizedek as a heavenly figure, but the writer of Hebrews calls him "like the Son of God" and not the same as him. Jesus is of Judah, not Levi, so the priesthood must change (7:11-14); the writer says the "order of Melchizedek" comes with an oath and lasts forever.

t: A better covenant: God will write his laws on their hearts
s: The writer says, "For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people."
n: The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. One of the longest Old Testament quotations in the New Testament (Jeremiah 31:31-34) is placed here. The writer says that the first covenant is "obsolete" and will "soon disappear" (8:13). Some scholars take that to mean the Temple still stood when the letter was written, and some think it was written after AD 70; the verses do not date the letter.

t: The earthly tabernacle and the Day of Atonement
s: The writer says, "When everything had been prepared in this way, the priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties. But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance."
n: The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. The writer describes the tent of Moses with a first room, the Holy Place, and an inner room, the Holy of Holies, entered only by the high priest once a year with blood (Leviticus 16). He lists the contents of the inner room in 9:4. Leviticus 16 and Exodus 25-30 do not say that the golden altar of incense stood in the inner room, and scholars discuss how verse 4 should be read.

t: Christ enters the heavenly sanctuary by his own blood
s: The writer says, "But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption."
n: The pin stands at the traditional site of the crucifixion, though the passage speaks of a heavenly sanctuary and does not name Golgotha. The writer contrasts the blood of goats and bulls with the blood of Christ and says that "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (9:22). Verse 16 uses the word diatheke, which can mean both "covenant" and "will," and the writer plays on both senses.

t: One sacrifice for all time
s: The writer says, "Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God."
n: The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. The priests stand daily and offer the same sacrifices, but Christ "sat down." The writer says the law is a "shadow" of the good things to come, and he quotes Psalm 40 with the Greek reading "a body You prepared for Me," which differs from the Hebrew, where the speaker says his ears were opened or dug out.

t: Draw near with a true heart; do not throw away your confidence
s: The writer says, "Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer recalls an earlier time when the readers were publicly exposed to abuse and sometimes shared the plight of others, and when they helped prisoners and accepted the loss of their goods. Some scholars connect this with the troubles of Jewish Christians in Rome about AD 49 under Claudius, others with other places and times. The letter does not say.

t: Faith defined: Abel, Enoch and Noah
s: The writer says, "Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended. By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible."
n: The pin stands in the mountains of Ararat, where Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest, as a general marker; the passage names no place and tells of Abel, Enoch and Noah. The chapter opens with the nearest thing in the Bible to a definition of faith. It then names heroes one at a time, and the words "By faith" begin most of the sentences that follow. The list is told from Genesis, the Law and the histories.

t: Abraham and Sarah: strangers in tents, looking for a city
s: The writer says, "By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God."
n: The pin stands at Mamre near Hebron, where Genesis 13:18 and 18:1 place Abraham's tents, though the passage speaks of him living "in tents" in the land generally. The writer says he went out "without knowing where he was going," lived as a stranger, and looked forward to a city with foundations, "whose architect and builder is God." Sarah is named as one who received power to conceive, and the offering of Isaac (verses 17-19) is told from Genesis 22.

t: By faith Moses, the Red Sea, Jericho and Rahab
s: The writer says, "By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient."
n: The pin stands at Jericho, where the walls fell and Rahab was spared, though the passage also tells of Moses' parents in Egypt, the Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea. The writer says Moses chose "to suffer oppression with God's people" and valued "disgrace for Christ" above the treasures of Egypt (11:25-26). Jericho's walls and the date of their fall are debated by archaeologists.

t: The faithful who suffered: a list of names and nameless
s: The writer says, "Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem as a general marker; the passage names six judges and prophets (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel) and then moves to unnamed people, some of whom were tortured, stoned or "sawed in two." Verse 35 ("women received back their dead" and others were tortured) fits the story of the mother and her seven sons in 2 Maccabees 6-7, though the letter does not name them. The tradition that Isaiah was sawn in two comes from a later Jewish text, the Martyrdom of Isaiah. The chapter ends by saying that they did not receive what was promised, so that "together with us" they might be made perfect.

t: A great cloud of witnesses: run with endurance
s: The writer says, "Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The race image would be familiar from the games at Isthmia, Corinth and elsewhere, and the writer speaks of throwing off "every encumbrance." The "cloud of witnesses" are the people of chapter 11, seen as those who have already run and now look on, though the writer does not say that they can see the readers. Jesus is the "author and perfecter" of faith and endured the cross, "scorning its shame."

t: The Lord disciplines the son he loves
s: The writer says, "And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: "My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.""
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 as words addressed to his readers as sons. In a Greek and Roman household a father trained and corrected his sons, and the writer uses that picture, saying that discipline is painful at the time and yields "a harvest of righteousness and peace" later. He adds that "you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood" (12:4).

t: Not Mount Sinai but Mount Zion
s: The writer says, "Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel."
n: The pin stands at Mount Zion in Jerusalem, though the writer means the heavenly Zion, the city of the living God. Verses 18-21 recall Mount Sinai, with fire, darkness, a trumpet and a voice so frightening that the people begged it to stop; the traditional Sinai (Jebel Musa) is only one of several proposed. The writer sets the "sprinkled blood" of Jesus above the blood of Abel, and calls for gratitude since "we are receiving an unshakable kingdom." Esau (12:16-17) is held up as a warning.

t: Let brotherly love continue: hospitality, prisoners, marriage, money
s: The writer says, "Continue in brotherly love. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The last chapter turns to daily life. Inns of the Roman world were rough and often unsafe, so travelers, including traveling Christian teachers, depended on private homes, which makes hospitality a matter of real need. The saying that some "have entertained angels" echoes Abraham and Sarah at Mamre (Genesis 18) and perhaps Lot (Genesis 19).

t: Outside the camp: Jesus suffered outside the gate
s: The writer says, "And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood. Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore."
n: The pin stands at the traditional site of the crucifixion, which the Gospels place outside the city (John 19:20). The writer says Jesus suffered "outside the city gate" to make the people holy through his own blood, as the bodies of the sin offering were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), and asks the readers to go to him "outside the camp." Verse 15 offers "a sacrifice of praise" in place of animal sacrifice, and verse 17 asks the readers to obey their leaders.

t: Timothy is free; greetings from Italy
s: The writer says, "Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings."
n: The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer. It ends with "Those from Italy send you greetings" (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer asks for prayer, hopes to be restored to the readers soon, and says that "our brother Timothy" has been released. This is likely Paul's coworker, though the letter does not give his name more fully, and nothing else says when he was imprisoned. The closing blessing and personal notes lead many to think of Paul, but the writing style, the use of the Greek Old Testament and the absence of the writer's name make the authorship an old question; Eusebius reports Origen as saying that only God knows who wrote it.

t: James greets the twelve tribes in the Dispersion
s: James writes, "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem, where the Book of Acts and Paul's letter to the Galatians place James, the brother of the Lord, as a leader of the church (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). The letter itself does not say where it was written. The writer calls himself "a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" and does not say he is the Lord's brother. The tradition that he is James the brother of Jesus is old and widely held; others have suggested a different James or a letter written in his name after his death. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of the stoning of James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, at the order of the high priest Ananus, about AD 62, so a letter from him would have to be earlier. The greeting uses the plain Greek word chairein, "Greetings," which Paul does not use in his letter openings but which opens the letters quoted in Acts 15:23 and 23:26.

t: Consider it pure joy when you meet trials
s: James writes, "Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance. Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything."
n: The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer's. It is addressed to "the twelve tribes of the Dispersion," which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The Greek word for "trials" (peirasmos) means both an outside test and an inner temptation, and James uses it both ways in this chapter (1:2, 12-14). The call to be glad in testing has parallels in Jesus' words in Matthew 5:11-12 and in Paul's and Peter's letters (Romans 5:3-4; 1 Peter 1:6-7). "Perseverance" (hypomone) is staying power under pressure, not a passive waiting.

t: Ask God for wisdom; the double-minded person
s: James writes, "Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind."
n: The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer's. It is addressed to "the twelve tribes of the Dispersion," which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. Wisdom is the main theme of Israel's wisdom books, and the story of Solomon asking for it is in 1 Kings 3. "Double-minded" translates dipsychos, literally two-souled. The word is not found in earlier Greek writing that survives, so James may have coined it or taken it from Jewish teaching; it returns in 4:8 and later fills the Shepherd of Hermas, a Christian writing of the 2nd century.

t: The lowly and the rich: the flower in the heat
s: James writes, "The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position. But the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field. For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits."
n: The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers' town nor its writer's.
