"Wake up" and "I will come like a thief" would have struck home. Nothing is said of persecution or false teaching here. The church has a good name and no life. A few have not soiled their clothes. White garments were worn at festivals and triumphs. The "Book of Life" is the roll of the citizens of God's city (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1); Greek cities kept such rolls and struck out the names of the condemned. Jesus promises to confess the overcomer's name before his Father (Matthew 10:32).

t: To the church in Philadelphia: an open door that no one can shut
s: John writes, "I know your deeds. See, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. For you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name."
n: Philadelphia, now Alaşehir, stood at the edge of a region of earthquakes. It was wrecked in AD 17 with Sardis, and for years many people lived outside the walls for fear of aftershocks. It took a new name, Neocaesarea, in thanks for the emperor's aid. To such a city Christ promises a pillar that will never be moved, a home no one will have to leave, and a new name. Like Smyrna, this church is small and receives no blame. The "key of David" comes from Isaiah 22:22, where a steward is given power over the king's house. The open door is probably the door into the kingdom, or an opening for mission. The promise to keep them "from the hour of testing" is read by some as removal before the trial and by others as protection through it (compare John 17:15). About AD 110 Ignatius wrote a letter to this church.

t: To the church in Laodicea: neither cold nor hot; I stand at the door and knock
s: John writes, "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me."
n: Laodicea was a banking and trading city in the Lycus valley, near Colossae and Hierapolis. After the earthquake of AD 60 it rebuilt from its own funds and refused help from Rome (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). It was known for glossy black wool and for an eye powder made in the region. So the church that says, "I am rich," is told it is poor, blind and naked, and is offered gold, white clothes and salve for its eyes. The city had no good spring. Water came by aqueduct and arrived tepid and full of lime, while Hierapolis had hot healing springs and Colossae cold fresh water. Lukewarm means useless, not half-hearted in feeling. This letter has no praise. Yet it has the warmest invitation: Christ stands at the door and knocks, and those he loves he corrects (Proverbs 3:12). "The Amen" as a title comes from Isaiah 65:16.

t: A door standing open in heaven: the throne, the elders and the four living creatures
s: John writes, "'Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The scene draws on Ezekiel 1, Isaiah 6 and Daniel 7. John does not describe the one on the throne except by the flash of precious stones and a rainbow (Genesis 9:13). Twenty-four elders in white with gold crowns sit around the throne. They have been taken as the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles together, as the whole people of God, or as an order of angels; the number also matches the twenty-four courses of priests in 1 Chronicles 24. The four living creatures, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, combine the cherubim of Ezekiel with the seraphim of Isaiah, and sing "Holy, Holy, Holy." The elders lay down their crowns, as subject kings did before the emperor. The words "our Lord and God" answer a title that the emperor Domitian is said to have claimed (Suetonius, Domitian 13). Everything that follows in the book is seen from this throne.

t: The scroll with seven seals and the Lamb who was slain
s: John writes, "And they sang a new song: 'Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. A scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals lies in God's right hand (compare Ezekiel 2:9-10). Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses. The scroll holds God's purpose for the world, and no one is found worthy to open it. John is told that the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Genesis 49:9-10; Isaiah 11:1, 10). He looks and sees a Lamb, standing as though it had been slain. This is the center of the book: the Lion wins as the Lamb, by his death. "Lamb" is used of Christ 28 times in Revelation. The seven horns stand for full power and the seven eyes for full knowledge (Zechariah 4:10). The new song says that by his blood he bought people for God from every tribe, tongue, people and nation. Praise spreads outward from the living creatures and elders to countless angels and then to every creature, and the Lamb is worshiped together with the one on the throne.

t: The first four seals: the four horsemen
s: John writes, "Then I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The colored horses come from Zechariah 1:8-11 and 6:1-8. The second, third and fourth riders bring war, famine and death. In the third seal a quart of wheat costs a denarius, a full day's pay for a day's bread for one person, many times the normal price; oil and wine are spared. The rider on the white horse with a bow and crown is read in opposite ways: as conquest or a false messiah, or as Christ or the advance of the gospel (compare 19:11). The order of the seals follows Jesus's words in Mark 13:7-9: wars, nations rising, famines, persecution, signs in the sky. Each rider "was given" his power, so nothing here is outside God's control. Christians read these visions in four main ways: as events of John's own time (preterist), as a map of church history (historicist), as events still to come at the end (futurist), or as pictures of a conflict that runs through every age (idealist). Many readers combine them.

t: The fifth seal: the souls under the altar cry, "How long?"
s: John writes, "And they cried out in a loud voice, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The blood of a sacrifice was poured at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7), so the picture means that those killed for the word of God have given their lives as an offering. "How long, O Lord?" is the cry of the Psalms (Psalm 79:5, 10; 94:3) and of Zechariah 1:12. It asks God to show that he is just. They are each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants who are to be killed is complete. John's first readers knew some names: Antipas at Pergamum (2:13), and before him those who died under Nero in Rome. The prayer is answered in 8:3-5, 16:5-7 and 19:2.

t: The sixth seal: the great day of wrath
s: John writes, "For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The earthquake, the black sun, the moon like blood, the falling stars and the sky rolled up are the language of the prophets for the day of the Lord (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 30-31; Haggai 2:6). Jesus uses it in Mark 13:24-25. Seven kinds of people, from kings to slaves, hide in caves and call on the mountains to fall on them (Hosea 10:8; Luke 23:30). The surprising phrase is "the wrath of the Lamb." The question that ends the chapter, "who is able to withstand it?", is answered in chapter 7. Christians read these visions in four main ways: as events of John's own time (preterist), as a map of church history (historicist), as events still to come at the end (futurist), or as pictures of a conflict that runs through every age (idealist). Many readers combine them.

t: The 144,000 sealed from the tribes of Israel
s: John writes, "And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel:"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Before the winds of judgment blow, God's servants are marked with a seal on their foreheads, as the faithful are marked in Ezekiel 9:4-6. The seal means ownership and protection; it is the counterpart of the mark of the beast in 13:16. The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand. The list of tribes is unusual: Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, comes first, Dan is left out, and both Joseph and Manasseh appear. Some readers take the 144,000 as Jewish believers, whether in John's day or at the end. Others take them as the whole church seen as the true Israel (compare James 1:1; Galatians 6:16) and the same people as the great multitude of verse 9, first heard as a number and then seen as a crowd, as the Lion was heard and the Lamb seen in chapter 5.

t: The great multitude that no one could count
s: John writes, "'Sir,' I answered, 'you know.' So he replied, 'These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. A crowd from every nation, tribe, people and tongue stands before the throne in white robes with palm branches, as at the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). It fulfills the promise to Abraham of offspring beyond counting (Genesis 15:5). They have come out of "the great tribulation" and have washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb. Some take the great tribulation as a final time of suffering before the end, others as the whole period of the church's suffering. The closing promises are from Isaiah 49:10 and 25:8: no hunger or thirst, the Lamb as their shepherd, springs of living water, and every tear wiped away. They return in 21:3-4.

t: The seventh seal: silence in heaven, and the prayers of the saints
s: John writes, "And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. When the last seal is opened there is silence for about half an hour, after the loud praise of chapters 4-7. It may be the hush before God acts (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:13), or silence so that the prayers can be heard. An angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, as the priest did each morning and evening in the temple (Exodus 30:1-8; Luke 1:9-10). Then he fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth (Ezekiel 10:2). The judgments that follow are shown as God's answer to the prayers of his people, including the "How long?" of 6:10.

t: The first four trumpets: earth, sea, rivers and sky are struck
s: John writes, "And as I observed, I heard an eagle flying overhead, calling in a loud voice, 'Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Trumpets were blown in Israel to sound an alarm, to gather the people and to announce the king (Numbers 10:1-10; Joel 2:1); seven trumpets brought down Jericho (Joshua 6). The first four recall the plagues on Egypt: hail and fire (Exodus 9:23-25), water turned to blood (7:20-21), darkness (10:21-23). Each strikes a third, so they are warnings and not the end; the bowls of chapter 16 will be complete. The star called Wormwood is named for a bitter plant (Jeremiah 9:15). An eagle then cries three woes for the three trumpets still to come. Some readers take the trumpets as events after the seals, and others as the same period shown again from another side, since both series end at the last day (6:12-17; 11:15-19).

t: The fifth trumpet: locusts from the Abyss
s: John writes, "They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. A star fallen from heaven is given the key to the shaft of the Abyss, the deep pit that is the prison of evil spirits (Luke 8:31). Smoke rises, and out of it come locusts like those of Joel 1-2 and the eighth plague of Egypt (Exodus 10:12-15). These do not eat plants. They torment for five months, about the life of a locust, only the people who do not have God's seal, and they are not allowed to kill. The description piles up comparisons: horses, crowns, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, scorpions' tails. Their king is the angel of the Abyss, named in Hebrew Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon, both meaning Destroyer. Some hear in the Greek name a jab at the god Apollo, whom Domitian honored.

t: The sixth trumpet: the armies released at the Euphrates
p: The Euphrates River (the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire)
s: John writes, "Now the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk."
n: The pin stands on the Euphrates, the one earthly place named in the vision. The river was the old border of the promised land (Genesis 15:18) and the road by which Assyria and Babylon had come. In John's day it was Rome's eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthians, whose mounted archers had beaten Roman armies. Four angels bound there are released to kill a third of mankind. The number of the mounted troops is "two hundred million," in the Greek two myriads of myriads, a number beyond counting. Fire, smoke and sulfur come from the horses' mouths. The point of the trumpets comes in the last two verses: the rest of mankind still did not repent of worshiping idols "of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood" (Daniel 5:23) or of murder, sorcery, immorality and theft. Warnings alone do not change hearts.

t: The mighty angel and the little scroll
s: John writes, "And I went to the angel and said, 'Give me the small scroll.' 'Take it and eat it,' he said. 'It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Between the sixth and seventh trumpets comes a pause, as between the sixth and seventh seals. A mighty angel wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow and a face like the sun, stands on sea and land holding a small open scroll. Seven thunders speak, and John is told to seal up what they said and not write it, the one thing in the book that is kept back. The angel swears, as in Daniel 12:7, that there will be no more delay: at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God will be finished. John eats the scroll, as Ezekiel did (Ezekiel 2:8-3:3). It is sweet as honey in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, because the message is God's word and yet it is a word of judgment and of suffering for the church. He must prophesy again about many peoples and kings.

t: The temple measured, and the two witnesses
s: John writes, "And I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.'"
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem. The witnesses lie dead in "the great city—figuratively called Sodom and Egypt—where their Lord was also crucified." John measures the temple and its worshipers, a sign of protection (Ezekiel 40-42; Zechariah 2:1-5), while the outer court is trampled for 42 months. That period is the same as the 1,260 days of verse 3 and the "time, and times, and half a time" of 12:14: three and a half years, from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, a limited time of trouble. Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth. They have the powers of Elijah (fire, no rain; 1 Kings 17:1) and Moses (water to blood, plagues), and are called two olive trees and two lampstands (Zechariah 4). They are killed by the beast from the Abyss, lie unburied three and a half days, are raised and taken up to heaven. Some take them as two prophets still to come, some as Moses and Elijah or Enoch and Elijah, and many as the witnessing church, since lampstands are churches in 1:20.

t: The seventh trumpet: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord
s: John writes, "Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. At the last trumpet loud voices in heaven announce that the rule of the world has passed to God and his Christ. Handel set the words in the "Hallelujah" chorus. The elders give thanks to God "the One who is and who was"; the words "is to come" are left out, because in the vision he has come. Their song sums up what the end brings: the nations raged (Psalm 2:1), God's wrath came, the dead are judged, his servants are rewarded, and those who destroy the earth are destroyed. God's temple in heaven is opened and the ark of the covenant is seen. The ark had been lost since Babylon destroyed the first temple in 586 BC; its appearing means that God keeps his covenant and that the way to his presence is open.

t: The woman clothed with the sun, the child and the great red dragon
s: John writes, "And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Chapters 12-14 go back and tell the story from the beginning as a conflict behind history. The woman with the sun, moon and twelve stars recalls Joseph's dream of Israel's family (Genesis 37:9-10). She is the people of God, from whom the Messiah comes, and after his birth her "other children" are the church (verse 17). Many Christians, especially in the Catholic tradition, also see Mary here. The dragon, named in verse 9 as the devil and Satan, has seven heads and ten horns like the beasts of Daniel 7. The child "who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter" is the Messiah of Psalm 2:9. His life is told in one line, birth and then being caught up to God's throne. The woman is fed in the wilderness for 1,260 days, as Israel was after the Exodus. People in Asia knew a myth of a dragon chasing a mother about to bear a god (Leto and Apollo); John tells the true version.

t: War in heaven: Michael and his angels fight the dragon
s: John writes, "They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Michael is the guardian angel of God's people in Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1. He and his angels throw the dragon out of heaven. The dragon is given all his names at once: the ancient serpent (Genesis 3), the devil (slanderer), Satan (adversary), the deceiver of the whole world. He is also "the accuser of our brothers," as in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1. The song explains what has happened: the accuser has lost his place because of the death of Christ. Believers have conquered him "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony." Jesus speaks of the same fall in Luke 10:18 and John 12:31. The devil has come down in great fury, "knowing he has only a short time." Some readers place this war before the creation of the world, and others at the very end; the song ties it to the cross.

t: The dragon pursues the woman and makes war on her children
s: John writes, "And the dragon was enraged at the woman, and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the dragon stood on the shore of the sea."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Thrown down to earth, the dragon chases the woman. She is given the two wings of a great eagle to fly to the wilderness, as God said he carried Israel on eagles' wings out of Egypt (Exodus 19:4). There she is fed for "a time, and times, and half a time" (Daniel 7:25). The serpent pours a river from his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth swallows it, as the sea and the earth swallowed Israel's enemies (Exodus 15:12). Unable to destroy her, the dragon goes to make war on "the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus." This explains to John's readers why they suffer: the enemy has already lost the main battle, and his attacks on them are the anger of the defeated. He takes his stand on the shore of the sea, and the next chapter shows the allies he calls up.

t: The beast from the sea
s: John writes, "Then the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 (lion, bear, leopard and a beast with ten horns), which stood for four empires. It is every empire that demands the worship due to God. It rises from the sea, as Roman governors arrived in Asia by ship. It gets its power from the dragon, has blasphemous names on its heads (emperors were called "lord," "savior" and "son of a god" on coins and inscriptions), and is worshiped by the whole world. One head seems to have been killed and its wound healed. Many connect this with the rumor, common after AD 68, that Nero had not died or would return; it is also a parody of the Lamb who was slain and lives. For John's first readers the beast was the Roman state in its claim to worship. Futurist readers see a final ruler, the Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). It is given 42 months and power to make war on the saints. Verse 10, from Jeremiah 15:2, calls for endurance and faith, not armed resistance.

t: The beast from the earth and the number 666
s: John writes, "Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. A second beast rises from the land, with two horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon. It is called the false prophet in 16:13 and 19:20. It makes people worship the first beast, does signs, and sets up an image that must be worshiped on pain of death, as in Daniel 3. For the first readers this fits the provincial council and local priests of Asia who organized the worship of the emperor. The mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell, is the opposite of God's seal (7:3; 14:1) and may echo Deuteronomy 6:8. The number of the beast "is the number of a man." In Greek and Hebrew, letters also stood for numbers. The most widely held solution is "Nero Caesar" written in Hebrew letters, which adds up to 666; the Latin spelling gives 616, and a few early copies, including Papyrus 115, read 616. Irenaeus, about AD 180, knew both numbers, offered other names, and advised against being sure. Others take 666 as falling short of the perfect seven three times over.

t: The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
s: John writes, "Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem, for Mount Zion. In the Psalms and prophets Zion is where God sets his king (Psalm 2:6) and gathers the rescued (Joel 2:32); Hebrews 12:22 uses the name for the heavenly city. After the two beasts and their mark, John sees the Lamb standing with the 144,000, who have his name and his Father's name on their foreheads. They sing a new song that only they can learn. They are called virgins who have not defiled themselves with women. Most take this as a picture of faithfulness, since the prophets call idolatry adultery and Israel's soldiers kept themselves apart for holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9-10; 1 Samuel 21:5); some take it literally. They "follow the Lamb wherever He goes," they are firstfruits to God, and no lie is found in their mouths (Zephaniah 3:13).

t: Three angels: the eternal gospel, Babylon fallen, and the warning
s: John writes, "And I heard a voice from heaven telling me to write, 'Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.' 'Yes,' says the Spirit, 'they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The first angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation: fear God, give him glory, worship the Maker of heaven and earth. The second announces, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great" (Isaiah 21:9), the first mention of Babylon in the book; chapters 17-18 fill it out. The third warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink the wine of God's anger, in words drawn from Isaiah 34:9-10 and the fate of Sodom. Verse 12 says what this requires of the saints: endurance, keeping God's commandments and their faith in Jesus. Then comes the second of the seven blessings: "Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on," and the Spirit answers that they will rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.

t: The harvest of the earth and the winepress of God's wrath
s: John writes, "Then another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the One seated on the cloud, 'Swing Your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest; for the crop of the earth is ripe.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. One like a son of man sits on a white cloud with a gold crown and a sharp sickle (Daniel 7:13). Two harvests follow, from Joel 3:13, where the sickle is put in because the harvest is ripe and the winepress is full. The grain harvest is taken by many as the gathering of God's people (Matthew 13:30; Mark 4:29) and by others as judgment. The grape harvest is plainly judgment: the grapes are thrown into the great winepress of God's wrath and trodden outside the city (Isaiah 63:1-6). Blood flows as high as a horse's bridle for 1,600 stadia, about 300 kilometers. Sixteen hundred is four times four times a hundred, a number for the whole earth. The picture returns in 19:15.

t: The song of Moses and of the Lamb, and seven angels with the last plagues
s: John writes, "and they sang the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb: 'Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations!"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Those who have conquered the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps. As Israel sang on the far shore of the Red Sea (Exodus 15), they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Its words are woven from the Old Testament (Psalm 86:9; 111:2; 145:17; Jeremiah 10:7; Deuteronomy 32:4), and it says nothing about the singers' own victory, only about God. All nations will come and worship him. The temple in heaven, called "the tabernacle of the Testimony," opens, and seven angels in bright linen receive seven golden bowls full of God's wrath. The temple fills with smoke from God's glory so that no one can enter, as at the dedication of the tabernacle and of Solomon's temple (Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11).

t: The first five bowls of wrath
s: John writes, "And I heard the altar reply: 'Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The bowls follow the pattern of the trumpets (earth, sea, rivers, sun, darkness) and of the plagues on Egypt: sores (Exodus 9:10), water to blood (7:17-21), darkness (10:21). The trumpets struck a third. The bowls strike everything, and they fall on those who have the mark of the beast and on its throne. In the middle the angel of the waters says that God is just: those who shed the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink. The altar answers, "Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments," the reply to the souls under the altar in 6:10. Three times John notes the response: people cursed God and did not repent. Christians read these visions in four main ways: as events of John's own time (preterist), as a map of church history (historicist), as events still to come at the end (futurist), or as pictures of a conflict that runs through every age (idealist). Many readers combine them.

t: The sixth bowl: the Euphrates dried up, and Armageddon
p: Megiddo (the place behind the name Armageddon)
s: John writes, "And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon."
n: The pin stands at Megiddo in northern Israel. "Armageddon" is most often explained as the Hebrew Har Megiddo, "mountain of Megiddo." Megiddo is a mound beside a wide plain, with no mountain of its own, where many battles were fought: Deborah and Barak (Judges 5:19), and King Josiah's death (2 Kings 23:29; Zechariah 12:11). The name stands for the place of the last gathering of the kings against God. Some expect a battle there; others take it as a symbol, since the battle itself is told in 19:11-21 with no place named. The Euphrates is dried up to open the way for the kings from the east, as Cyrus took Babylon by turning the river (Isaiah 44:27-28; Jeremiah 50:38). Three unclean spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet to gather the kings. In the middle Jesus speaks: "Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake," the third blessing of the book.

t: The seventh bowl: "It is done!"
s: John writes, "Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, 'It is done!'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The last bowl is poured on the air, and a loud voice from the throne says, "It is done!" Lightning, thunder and the greatest earthquake in human history follow, the same signs that closed the seals and the trumpets (8:5; 11:19). The great city splits into three parts, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembers Babylon the great. Islands flee and mountains disappear. Hailstones weighing about a talent, roughly 35 to 45 kilograms, fall on people (Exodus 9:22-26; Joshua 10:11), and they curse God. The fall of Babylon, stated here in a sentence, is shown at length in chapters 17 and 18.

t: The great prostitute on the scarlet beast
p: Rome (the city on seven hills; one reading of “Babylon”)
s: John writes, "And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH."
n: The pin stands at Rome, a judgment call. The woman sits on seven hills (17:9) and is "the great city that rules over the kings of the earth" (17:18), which in John's day could only mean Rome, the city of seven hills. A coin of Vespasian struck in AD 71 shows the goddess Roma seated on seven hills, and 1 Peter 5:13 also calls Rome "Babylon," the old empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, as Rome did in AD 70. Other readings take Babylon as unfaithful Jerusalem, as a city or system still to come, or as every proud power that grows rich by injustice. The prophets called Tyre and Nineveh prostitutes for seducing nations with their trade and power (Isaiah 23:16-17; Nahum 3:4). She is dressed in purple and scarlet with gold and pearls, holds a golden cup, and is drunk with the blood of the saints. John is carried to a wilderness to see her, and later to a high mountain to see the bride (21:9-10): the book sets two women and two cities side by side.

t: The mystery of the woman and the beast explained
p: Rome (the city on seven hills; one reading of “Babylon”)
s: John writes, "They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.'"
n: The pin stands at Rome, for the seven hills of verse 9. An angel explains the vision, and the explanation is itself hard. The beast "was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss," a mockery of the God "who is and was and is to come." The seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings: five have fallen, one is, and one is yet to come. Attempts to match these to Roman emperors disagree about where to start counting and whether to include the three who ruled briefly in AD 68-69; seven may simply stand for the full line of rulers. The ten horns are ten kings who receive power for "one hour" with the beast. They make war on the Lamb, "and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings." In the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman and destroy her, so that evil destroys itself, and God's purpose is carried out by it.

t: Fallen is Babylon the great: come out of her, my people
p: The ruins of Babylon on the Euphrates
s: John writes, "Then I heard another voice from heaven say: 'Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues."
n: The pin stands at the ruins of ancient Babylon on the Euphrates, whose fall in 539 BC is the model for this chapter. The prophets' songs over Babylon (Isaiah 13; 21; 47; Jeremiah 50-51) and over Tyre (Ezekiel 26-28) supply nearly every line. A shining angel announces the fall as already done. The city has become a haunt of demons and unclean birds (Isaiah 13:21-22). Three charges are made: she led the nations into immorality, the kings shared it, and the merchants grew rich from her luxury. "Come out of her, My people" repeats Jeremiah 51:45. For the first readers it meant refusing a share in the idolatry and injustice of the empire while still living in its cities. She says, "I sit as queen; I am not a widow" (Isaiah 47:7-8), and her plagues come in a single day.

t: The kings, the merchants and the seafarers mourn
p: Rome (the city on seven hills; one reading of “Babylon”)
s: John writes, "And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo—"
n: The pin stands at Rome, the city whose trade this passage describes. Three groups stand far off and cry, "Woe, woe": the kings, the merchants and all who work the sea, as in Ezekiel's lament for Tyre (Ezekiel 27). Each says that her ruin came "in a single hour." The merchants weep "because there is no one left to buy their cargo." The cargo list has 28 items, arranged from gold and jewels through fine cloth, scented wood, ivory, spices, wine, oil, wheat, cattle, horses and carriages. Nearly all are known from Roman writers as luxury imports. The list ends with "slaves and souls of men" (in the Greek, bodies and human lives): people traded as goods, placed last as the worst item on the bill. A large part of the people of Rome and Italy were slaves, and the grain fleet from Egypt fed the city. Wealth built on such trade is what the chapter condemns.

t: The millstone thrown into the sea
s: John writes, "Then a mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: 'With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. A mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea and says that Babylon will be thrown down in the same way, never to be found again. Jeremiah had a scroll tied to a stone and sunk in the Euphrates as a sign against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:63-64). A poem follows of what will never again be heard or seen in her: harpists and flute players, craftsmen, the sound of a mill, the light of a lamp, the voice of bridegroom and bride (Jeremiah 25:10). Heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are told to rejoice, because God has judged her for the way she treated them. The last verse gives the deepest charge: in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who have been slain on the earth.

t: Hallelujah! The marriage supper of the Lamb
s: John writes, "Then the angel told me to write, 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' And he said to me, 'These are the true words of God.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. "Hallelujah," Hebrew for "Praise the Lord," occurs four times here and nowhere else in the New Testament. Heaven praises God because his judgments are true and just. Then the theme changes from the fallen city to a wedding. The prophets spoke of God as the husband of his people (Isaiah 54:5-6; Hosea 2:19-20), and Jesus spoke of himself as the bridegroom and of the kingdom as a wedding feast (Mark 2:19-20; Matthew 22:1-14). The bride has made herself ready, and yet her fine linen "was given" to her; it stands for the righteous acts of the saints. The fourth blessing follows: "Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." John falls down to worship the angel and is stopped: "I am a fellow servant... Worship God!" The same thing happens in 22:8-9. Angels are not to be worshiped.

t: The rider on the white horse: King of kings and Lord of lords
s: John writes, "And He has a name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. Heaven stands open, and Christ appears as a rider called Faithful and True, who judges and makes war with justice (Isaiah 11:4). His eyes are like fire, as in 1:14. He wears many crowns, and has a name no one knows but himself, and the name "The Word of God" (John 1:1). His robe is dipped in blood before any battle is described. Some take this as the blood of his enemies, from Isaiah 63:1-3, and others as his own blood. The armies of heaven follow in white linen and carry no weapons. The only weapon is the sharp sword from his mouth, his word. He will rule the nations with an iron scepter (Psalm 2:9) and tread the winepress of God's wrath (14:19-20). On his robe and thigh is written "KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS," a title claimed by the kings of Babylon and Persia (Ezekiel 26:7; Daniel 2:37).

t: The beast and the false prophet are captured
s: John writes, "But the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. An angel standing in the sun calls the birds to "the great supper of God," a grim counterpart to the marriage supper of the Lamb. The picture is from Ezekiel 39:17-20, the feast after the defeat of Gog. The beast and the kings of the earth gather their armies against the rider. No fighting is described. The beast is seized, and with it the false prophet who did signs on its behalf; both are thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. The rest are killed by the sword from the rider's mouth. This is the gathering of 16:14-16, called Armageddon. Futurist readers expect a real final battle at Christ's return. Others take it as a picture of his victory by his word over every power that opposes him.

t: Satan bound, and the thousand years
s: John writes, "Blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with Him for a thousand years."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. An angel binds the dragon with a great chain and shuts him in the Abyss for a thousand years, so that he cannot deceive the nations. John sees thrones, and the souls of those beheaded for their witness to Jesus come to life and reign with Christ a thousand years. This is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of the thousand years, called the millennium, and Christians have understood it in three main ways. Premillennial readers hold that Christ returns before it and reigns on earth; this was the view of Papias, Justin and Irenaeus in the 2nd century and is widely held today. Amillennial readers, following Augustine, take it as the present age between Christ's first and second comings, when Satan is restrained (Mark 3:27) and the faithful dead reign with Christ in heaven. Postmillennial readers expect a long age of the gospel's success before Christ returns. All agree on the fifth blessing in verse 6: over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power.

t: Satan released, Gog and Magog, and the lake of fire
s: John writes, "And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, into which the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. When the thousand years end, Satan is released and goes out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, "Gog and Magog," and gather them for battle. The names come from Ezekiel 38-39, where Gog of the land of Magog leads a host from the far north against Israel after its restoration. Here they stand for all the nations. They surround "the camp of the saints and the beloved city," and fire comes down from heaven and consumes them. Again no battle is described. The devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet already are. The enemies are removed in the reverse of the order in which they appeared: Babylon, the two beasts, and last the dragon who stood behind them. Those who take the thousand years as the present age see this as the same battle as 19:17-21 told again.

t: The great white throne and the book of life
s: John writes, "And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And there were open books, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. John sees a great white throne, and earth and sky flee from the presence of the one seated on it. The dead, great and small, stand before the throne, and books are opened (Daniel 7:9-10). The dead are judged by what they have done, as recorded in the books (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Another book is opened, the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3), and it decides who enters the city. The sea, Death and Hades give up their dead, so that no one is beyond reach of this judgment. Then Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire. Paul calls death the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). This is the second death. Anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire.

t: A new heaven and a new earth: God will dwell with them
s: John writes, "'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.'"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 is fulfilled. John adds that "the sea was no more." In this book the sea is where the beast came from and what kept John on Patmos from his churches. The holy city comes down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride. A loud voice says that God's dwelling is now with mankind. The word for "dwell" is the word for the tabernacle (Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; John 1:14). He will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning or pain (Isaiah 25:8). Then God himself speaks from the throne, for only the second time in the book: "Behold, I make all things new." He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty (Isaiah 55:1) and warns that the cowardly, the unbelieving and the rest have their place in the lake of fire.

t: The new Jerusalem, the bride, the wife of the Lamb
s: John writes, "But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple."
n: The pin stands at Jerusalem, whose name the new city bears. One of the angels who showed John the prostitute now shows him the bride, and she is a city. It shines like jasper. Its twelve gates carry the names of the tribes of Israel and its twelve foundations the names of the apostles of the Lamb, so that the people of both covenants are one city (Ezekiel 48:30-35; Ephesians 2:20). It measures 12,000 stadia, about 2,200 kilometers, in length, width and height. The only other perfect cube in the Bible is the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20): the whole city is the place of God's presence. The twelve foundation stones recall the stones on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20), each gate is a single pearl, and the street is gold. John sees no temple, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple." It needs no sun; the nations walk by its light and bring their glory in, and its gates are never shut (Isaiah 60).

t: The river of the water of life and the tree of life
s: John writes, "down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The last vision returns to the garden of Genesis 2-3. A river clear as crystal flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the street (Ezekiel 47:1-12; Zechariah 14:8). On each side stands the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, one each month, and "the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations." The way to that tree was closed in Genesis 3:24, and here it is open. "No longer will there be any curse" reverses Genesis 3:14-19. His servants will see his face, which no one could do and live (Exodus 33:20), and his name will be on their foreheads. There will be no night, and they will reign forever and ever. The Bible's story began in a garden and ends in a garden city.

t: "Behold, I am coming soon": the last words of the vision
s: John writes, "The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!' Let the one who hears say, 'Come!' And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely."
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. The closing section is a set of short sayings from the angel, from John and from Jesus. Three times Jesus says, "I am coming soon" (verses 7, 12, 20). The sixth and seventh blessings are here: on the one who keeps the words of this prophecy, and on those who wash their robes. Daniel was told to seal up his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4). John is told not to seal his, because the time is near. Jesus calls himself the Alpha and the Omega, a title given to God in 1:8, and "the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star" (Numbers 24:17; Isaiah 11:1). Verse 17 is an open invitation: the Spirit and the bride say, "Come!", and whoever is thirsty may take the water of life freely.

t: A warning, a prayer and a blessing: "Come, Lord Jesus!"
s: John writes, "He who testifies to these things says, 'Yes, I am coming soon.' Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!"
n: The pin stands at Patmos, where John says he received the visions (1:9). What he sees here is set in heaven or in vision, and has no place on a map. John warns everyone who hears the book read not to add to it or take away from it, in the manner of Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32. The warning protects this prophecy as it is copied and read aloud. Jesus says a last time, "Yes, I am coming soon," and the church answers, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" This is the Greek form of the Aramaic prayer Marana tha, "Our Lord, come," which the first Christians used at the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 16:22; Didache 10.6). The book ends as a letter does, with a blessing of grace. It is the last sentence of the Bible. Revelation was accepted early in the West. In the East some doubted it for centuries: Dionysius of Alexandria questioned its author, Eusebius was undecided, the early Syriac Bible lacked it, and it is still not read in the public services of the Eastern Orthodox churches.
